text:
Don’t wait for more poles to close the holes.
By then the Fourth is already gone.

Missing children and stolen cars matter. Nobody serious is cheering for the next abduction.

The fight is not “cops vs chaos.” It is this product: cameras on the road that photograph every passing car — plate, time, place, color, stickers — and store that so police can search it later and share it. You were not a suspect when the pole clicked. You were driving.

There’s no way to rule innocent men — until every car has a trail. Then you don’t invent the person. You search for him.

Flock advocates say it is just a public plate. A cop on the corner could write the same number down. That is one look. This is a file that lasts and spreads. Police already look up who owns a plate. The camera hands them the number. The vehicle registration file hands them the name. The state’s license photo — the clear picture REAL ID made every state keep — sits in another drawer. The same government agency can open both. Two files on paper becomes one person in practice.

Flock advocates point to court cases about one town’s cameras with gaps in coverage and say the Fourth Amendment is settled. Those cases did not bless a growing shared net, or a search weeks later, or the owner lookup. A small ruling is not a big permission slip.

Flock advocates say the tool saves lives, so you wanting to impose limits means you want the grave. That is a false choice. You can want the child found and still refuse a default file on everybody. The third path is a tighter tool: short storage of all data, no extra traffic product the city never bought, no hundred searches on a man who legally filmed a cop.

Flock advocates say the fences are easy. Wisconsin deputies ran this system more than a hundred times on a Navy veteran after he recorded a stop. Sheboygan was offered years of speed and travel data it says it never approved. A log after the fact is not a lock on the door. If the tool is that handy, officials will go around the fence.

Now add software that can comb those unlocked files all at once — every plate, every time, every owner record the agency can already open — and the person at the login does not need a hunch. They need a purpose. If that purpose is control, not a single crime, the machine will serve it. Flock advocates still talk like a deputy is typing one plate for one case. A system that can sweep the linked drawers is not that deputy. It is a staff that never sleeps.

The American experiment assumed the government would have to pick a target before it got the story of your week. This stack works the other way: story first, target when needed. That is not a better flashlight. That is the end of living as someone the state has not already filed.

The Fourth Amendment is supposed to stop a bad search habit before it becomes furniture. Waiting until the holes in the map fill with more poles means you act when the tool is too useful to unwind. That is not caution. That is delay.

Do not build a memory of the innocent because the first ad was a victim. Do not pretend the drawers stay apart when the same hands hold both keys. Do not hand those hands a searcher that never gets bored. Do not wait for the holes to close.

Don’t wait for more poles to close the holes.
By then the Fourth is already gone.

text:
In 1958, a computer learned to distinguish punch cards marked on the left from cards marked on the right. After roughly 50 training attempts, it could classify them without error.

The next morning, The New York Times reported that the U.S. Navy expected the eventual machine to "walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence."

Eleven years later, neural networks were widely being treated as a dead end.

Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron had been misunderstood in both directions.

Rosenblatt was a 29-year-old psychologist at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory. Computing had entered his work through an unusual route => as a graduate student studying personality, he built a machine called EPAC to process psychological test data and nicknamed it the "Idiot Brain."

His larger interest was biological. How could a brain recognize something it had never seen in exactly that form before? How could experience change the way it responded next time?

Earlier researchers had supplied parts of the answer. Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts had described simplified neurons as threshold logic units. Donald Hebb had proposed that learning involved changes in the strength of connections between neurons. Rosenblatt combined this lineage with an error-correction procedure and built a trainable system for recognizing patterns.

The perceptron received an input, combined signals through weighted connections and produced a response. During training, a correct response left the relevant weights alone; an error caused them to be adjusted. For any binary classification problem that could be separated by a linear boundary, the learning procedure was guaranteed to find such a boundary after a finite number of corrections.

The 1958 demonstration took place in software on an IBM 704. The purpose-built Mark I Perceptron followed and was publicly demonstrated in 1960.

Its visual input came from a camera containing a 20×20 grid of photocells. The 400 sensory units connected to 512 association units, which fed eight binary response units. Each sensory unit could connect to as many as 40 association units, with the wiring commonly chosen from tables of random numbers.

The trainable connections were controlled by motor-driven potentiometers. Updating a weight meant physically rotating an electrical component inside the machine.

This was the part obscured by all the talk of electronic brains. Rosenblatt had demonstrated a different way of programming. Instead of specifying the complete recognition rule, the designer supplied examples and a procedure for learning from errors. The resulting behaviour was stored across the machine’s adjustable connections.

The distinction between training and programming is ordinary to us now. It was not ordinary in 1958.

The perceptron’s limitations were real. The basic classifier learned only a linear decision boundary. AND and OR could be represented this way, but XOR could not => its positive examples lie on diagonally opposite corners, so no single straight line can separate them from the negative examples.

In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published Perceptrons. They rigorously analysed restricted perceptron architectures and showed serious limitations on problems such as parity and determining whether regions in an image were connected. They also doubted that adding trainable layers would provide a practical escape.

The book arrived after enthusiasm had already begun to fade. Early results had not justified the publicity, computers were severely constrained, effective training of multiple adaptive layers remained unresolved, and funding priorities were changing. Its publication helped solidify the belief that neural networks offered little room for progress, but it did not mathematically prove that every neural-network architecture was useless.

Rosenblatt knew that the simple perceptron was inadequate for many problems. His 1962 book examined multilayer and cross-coupled systems while openly listing the difficulties that still had to be solved. His disagreement with Minsky, a former schoolmate from the Bronx High School of Science, was not over whether the early machines were limited. It was over whether those limits justified abandoning the approach.

Rosenblatt died in a sailing accident in Chesapeake Bay on July 11, 1971, his 43rd birthday. He did not live through the revival of neural-network research in the 1980s.

Earlier formulations of backpropagation already existed, but the influential 1986 work of David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams demonstrated how it could train hidden layers to develop useful internal representations. Subsequent advances in architectures, data and computing power pushed neural networks far beyond anything the Mark I could do.

Modern Transformers bear little architectural resemblance to Rosenblatt’s machine. They use attention, differentiable nonlinearities and gradient-based optimization across enormous parameter spaces. The shared principle is more fundamental: useful behaviour can be learned by adjusting a network’s internal connections in response to data.

Once the 1958 hype and the later dismissal are removed, Rosenblatt’s achievement needs little embellishment. He built an early working learning system and helped turn adaptation from examples into an engineering discipline.

Modern AI grew from taking that possibility seriously.

That is the part that bothers me. Because it is easy to put a camera in front of a tragedy and tell the public who the heroes are. It is easy to show a dead baby, a dumpster, police tape, grieving relatives and a reporter standing outside the scene. It is easy to tell people that an organization is helping children and families. Olive Crest publicly describes its mission as strengthening, equipping and restoring children and families in crisis, and its Nevada operation openly describes programs involving foster families, family preservation, mental health and other services. Fine. Those services can be evaluated on their actual performance. But Project Stone is not interested in the commercial. Project Stone is interested in the paper trail.

So give me the call. Give me the timestamp. Give me the incident number. Give me the dispatch. Give me the referral. Give me the intake record. Give me the policy that authorized the referral. Give me the contract governing the service. Give me the funding source. Give me the database entry. Give me the access log. Give me the retention policy. Give me the records-request response. Give me the explanation for every redaction. Give me the explanation for every withheld record. If the system worked, then show how it worked. If the system failed, show where it failed. If somebody made a mistake, identify the mistake. If somebody violated a policy, identify the policy. If somebody committed a crime, then investigate the crime. But don’t expect the public to accept a television narrative as a substitute for an audit trail.

And now let’s turn that demand into an actual records investigation, because this is where Project Stone stops being just a monologue and becomes a fucking records trail. First, lock down the exact date range. Don’t send somebody a request saying “give me everything about Olive Crest.” Make it specific: identify the incident date, the approximate time, the location, the agency, the program, the telephone number, the case number if known and the people or departments believed to have handled the matter. Clark County itself advises requesters to be as specific as possible, provide a date range and identify the departments or employees who may have been involved.

Second, make the 911 request separately from the child-welfare request. Ask the appropriate emergency-services custodian for the call-for-service record, CAD event, incident number, dispatch timeline, disposition, audio if releasable, and any releasable associated records for the specific date and time. Don’t mix ten different agencies into one request and then wonder why nobody knows who owns the record. Identify the actual custodian. Clark County specifically notes that it is not the custodian of police, detention or court records and directs requesters to the appropriate law-enforcement agency for those records.

Third, make a separate request for 311 or other non-emergency county records if that system is involved. Ask for the call number, date and time, originating department, disposition, referral destination, associated service request and any releasable metadata. The point is not to demand somebody else’s private information. The point is to establish whether a particular call existed, where it went and what governmental system received it.

Fourth, make a separate request to Clark County Department of Family Services. And this is where the law matters. Clark County currently states that its CPS records and agency files are confidential and cites NRS 432B.280 and NRS 127.200. DFS also explains that certain people, including a child, parent or guardian, a subject of a report, their attorney, or a person with a court order, may have access under NRS 432B.290. For eligible requesters, DFS offers a case-closure-summary request and a general-records request, and it warns that records may be redacted and that submitting a request does not guarantee access to the entire file.

text:
There is a form of property ownership where you can never be taxed out of your own home.

It's called allodial title.

Total ownership. No landlord. Not even the government.

Compare that to what you have right now.

Fee simple title, the standard in America, means you're always a renter with extra steps.

Miss enough property tax payments on a house you paid off 20 years ago and the county takes it. Doesn't matter if your mortgage has been gone for decades.

You never actually stop paying rent. You just pay it to a different landlord.

Here's the part that should make you angry.

Nevada actually built a program for this in 1997.

Homeowners could pay a lump sum covering their future property taxes and receive a certificate of allodial title. No more annual tax bill. Ever.

For almost a decade, real Americans held title to their homes the way our ancestors once did before feudal systems bled into modern property law.

Then in 2005, Nevada shut it down.

Officially they called it "actuarially unsound."

Unofficially, imagine the tax revenue a state loses when homeowners stop paying forever instead of paying annually. Now imagine every state watching what Nevada did.

That program never had a chance of spreading. It threatened the entire business model of property taxation.

No state has offered it since. None currently do.

But the fact that it existed even once should make you ask a bigger question.

What would it take to bring it back?

Because if true ownership was possible for a few years in Nevada, it's possible again.

American heavyweight Duane Bobick, who'd bested Nick Wells and Larry Holmes (in a box-off on August 5th) to earn his spot in Munich, is TKO'd in the 3rd round of his Olympic Quarter-Final bout against legendary Cuban boxer Teofilo Stevenson on September 6, 1972. 

Bobick, dropped three times in that 3rd round after a very competitive first two rounds, had previously defeated Stevenson at the 1971 Pan American Games.
----------------------------------------------------------
From British Vintage boxing on perhaps the greatest amateur boxer of all-time, Teofilo Stevenson of Cuba:

'What are eight million dollars compared to the love of eight million Cubans.’
- Teofilo  Stevenson
The above quote was in response to a very lucrative offer, to turn professional after Stevenson’s second consecutive Olympic heavyweight gold medal, at the 1976 Games. The offer was actually nearer $5 million dollars to fight nonother than Muhammad Ali. In essence, The Greatest fighting the greatest.
Despite the best efforts from the likes of Bob Arum and Don King, it was a fight which unfortunately never materialised and one which many tipped Stevenson to win. A similar offer was made a few years later to Stevenson’s successor, Félix Savón, to fight Mike Tyson and again, the offer was turned down, despite a ludicrous amount of money being offered and Savón being the favourite. So why exactly did possibly Cuba’s most famous athletes of all time turn down such life changing sums of cash? The answer is, morals and integrity……with a little bit of influencing. Also, the media and politicians decided to stick their oar in and make it a battle between Cuban Communism versus American Democracy, which certainly didn’t help to bring the fight to fruition.
It's a debate which will continue for years. Who would win? Stevenson had all the tools and power to dismantle Ali, yet, he had been primed his whole life for three round contests, under different rules. Ali on the other hand was himself an Olympic gold medallist and had been in with some of the hardest punchers in history in the pro ranks. Who would have won? We’ll never know.
Professional boxing was banned in Cuba from 1962, due to their then leader, Fidel Castro regarding the sport as corrupt and consequently convincing his fellow Cubans to compete for the glory of representing their country instead of their bank balance. As a result, many great Cuban boxers never got to test their full potential under professional rules and many others left their home country, changed nationalities and fought under the banner of other countries. 
Back to Teófilo. Another reason he declined the offer to fight Ali in 1976, is because his work in the amateur ring was far from over and he would go on to raise the bar to unparalleled heights.
Teófilo Stevenson Lawrence was Cuban born, but the exact whereabouts of his birth has never fully been confirmed. Puerto Padre is the most common answer, however, Las Tunas has also been in the mix, as has Jamaica. All we do know is that he was born on 29 March 1952.
Teófilo ’s mother, Dolores was first generation Cuban, from St Kitts heritage, whereas his father, Teófilo Stevenson Patterson, an immigrant from Saint Vincent, worked the docks and took on a number of jobs to pay the bills, including teaching English.
Stevenson Sr was a large frame of a man and had a passion for training and sparring in boxing gyms. Despite having a rumoured 10 fights as an amateur, his dislike of the payment for boxers made him give up and concentrate on gaining a trade.
However, it was Sr’s involvement in the square ring that inspired young Stevenson to lace up the gloves at nine years of age. Under the tutelage of former light heavyweight national champion, John Herrera, Stevenson started to rack up the silverware and by 1968 won gold at the Cuba Junior Championships, at light middleweight.
A knockout victory over Nancio Carrillo gained the attention of the onlookers, due to Carillo having represented Cuba at the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City. It was at this point Cuba hired in some help from the East.
Stevenson’s learning curve went vertical when he started training in Havana with the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) coach, Andrei Chervonenko, who had set up a boxing school in the country’s capital. Up to this point, Stevenson’s style was based more under the fundamentals of professional boxing, whereas Chervonenko showed him how to win fights under the amateur scoring system, through his vast experience of success with some of the best Eastern European fighters at the time.
By the age of 17, Stevenson was now boxing in the senior ranks, albeit, the vastly talented Cuban started off with two points losses against Adolfo Galvez (1986) and Gabriel Garcia (1969), in the Playa Giron - Cuban National Championships.
However, in 1970, Stevenson beat Earl McClear to win the Central American and Caribbean Championships, followed by a trip to Bulgaria, where he won three fights in six days to win the Friendship Tournament Heavyweight crown.  
In 1971, Stevenson reached the finals of the Pan American Games in Colombia, falling short against the highly talented American, Duane Bobick (the same man who would deny Larry Holmes passage to the 1972 USA Olympic Team). Stevenson did however pick up the bronze medal and the same year travelled to Germany to win the TSC tournament and also won the Playa Giron - Cuban National Championships once again.
One year later and Stevenson locked horns with Bobick again, in what was simply an outstanding fight. In 12 months, Stevenson was simply a different beast. Physically, mentally and technically, he was displaying traits of a legend in the making. On this occasion, they were paired at the 1972 Olympic Games at Munich in the quarter finals.
As the fight moved into the third and decisive final round, Stevenson floored the defiantly good, Bobick three times and in doing so progressed to the semifinals, to face German, Peter Hussing.
After smashing the German in the second round, (who claimed to have never been hit so hard before) Stevenson went on to pick up gold and consequently become the Olympic heavyweight champion, after Romanian, Ion Alexe was unable to make the final due to a broken hand. For the small number of naysayers who claimed Stevenson was gifted his prize, he would go on to prove that he was indeed, no fluke. In fact, the 1972 Olympics was to mark an unprecedented run of amateur brilliance beyond the next decade.
Stevenson despatches Peter Hussing in the semi-finals 1972 Olympic Games
In addition to his coveted Olympic gold, in the very same year, Stevenson also went on to receive the Val Barker Trophy and the Merited Master of Sport of the USSR, which is an honour rarely awarded to non-Russian nationals.
Two years later, Cuba awarded Stevenson two large houses for his continued successes in the ring, which came under attack from the AIBA president, Anwar Choudry, claiming that this practice did not run along the guidelines of the amateur system. The Cuban officials responded by saying that’s how they rewarded their athletes. End of story.
Stevenson went on to win the World Championships in 1974 in front of adorning fans in Havana, Cuba, followed by Gold at the Pan American Games in 1975.  Between 1973 – 1976, Stevenson’s only losses came at the hands of Russian, Igor Yvsotsky, which included his only ever knockout loss. Incredibly, despite 161 victories as an amateur, Yvsotsky would never compete at the Olympics.
In the summer of 1976, Stevenson wowed fans in Montreal, Canada, with a string of glowing performances, stopping the big Fin, Pekka Ruokola and future professional world heavyweight champion, John Tate in the semifinal. Former world heavyweight champion, George Foreman was commentating ringside and he was asked if he believed Stevenson had what it took to make the transition to the pro ranks. Foreman responded, ‘I haven’t seen that much class and skill in amateur or professional boxing! In my opinion, Stevenson would undoubtedly become the world heavyweight boxing champion, because he has the skill and qualifications.’
Funnily enough, comparisons of Stevenson were often made with both Foreman and Ali, in terms of having the speed, footwork and agility of Ali, whilst possessing similar power to Foreman. Standing at 6ft 4 inches, with an abundance of talent, in boxing terms, he was the complete nightmare package to meet in the ring.
After dispatching Tate, Stevenson forced Romanian, Mircea Simonto to retire in the third round of the final. He was now a double gold medal Olympian. Over 30 years later, Stevenson told Associated Press, ‘The Olympic Games in Munich and Montreal are the fondest memories I have from my life, the best stage of my career.’
Four years later, USA boycotted the Olympics in Moscow and although his route to gold was not easy, but let’s say it was ‘easier.’ Stevenson won his first two fights by stoppage, beating Hungarian Istvan Levai in the semifinal, then winning gold by beating Piotr Zaev of the Soviet Union. Although the boycotting is something which worked in Stevenson’s favour on this occasion, it turned out to be his arch enemy for the next two Olympic Games.
In 1982, Stevenson lost to Italian, Francesco Damiani at the World Championships, which scuppered his consecutive trilogy run of golds at this tournament. The Italian went on to claim silver and then two years later also gained silver on the Olympic podium in Los Angeles, at the 1984 summer Olympiad. Damiani turned professional in January 1985 and went on to become European and WBO world heavyweight champion, with a very respectable pro record of 30-2, with the two losses coming at the hands of Ray Mercer and Oliver McCall. The loss against Damiani denied Stevenson the possibility of four golds on the bounce in the World Championships.
Over the next four years, Stevenson continued to create a blaze of success, gaining gold at the Friendship Games in 1984 and a further third gold at the World Championships in 1986 in Reno, Nevada. Sadly, politics has a way of affecting the trajectory of success for so many athletes and the 1984 Olympics was no different for Stevenson, as Cuba boycotted the games. Tyrell Biggs, who Stevenson had defeated shortly before, in a Cuba versus USA tournament, went on to win the Olympic super heavyweight gold medal, which was the first time this weight class had been introduced. Once again, Stevenson was denied the chance to gain four gold medals in four consecutive major tournaments. In fact, Stevenson may well have had a chance of gaining five gold medals, had Cuba also not boycotted the 1988 Olympics in Seoul.  The boycott was the straw breaking the camel’s back for Stevenson and he retired shortly after Cuba’s withdrawal in 1988.
Although denied the chance to expand his collection of Olympic medals, in 1987, Stevenson was awarded the highly prestigious Olympic Order, which is the most distinguished award for any athlete to be awarded by the International Olympic Committee, for their contribution to sport.
Stevenson retired with a sensational amateur boxing record of 302 wins, 22 losses and eight draws, although folklore has Stevenson fighting in as many as 600 amateur contests. However, it’s not just the wins, it’s the calibre of the fights he was in, the opposition he defeated and the way he did it.
Hungarian László Papp was the first boxer to win three consecutive gold medals in the Olympics, however, Stevenson, the second to reach such fistic heights, made history by being the first to win three consecutive golds in the heavyweight ranks. Add fellow Cuban, Félix Savón into the group and the trio are the only triple consecutive Olympic boxing gold medallists in boxing history.
Stevenson went on to live in Havana, became part of the coaching detail within the national squad and held the coveted position of vice president of Cuba’s Boxing Federation. Sadly, he  died from complications relating to heart disease on 11 June 2012, in Havana Cuba. He was only 60 years old and was survived by his two children.
With what he achieved in the ring from 1966 - 1986, a lifespan of perhaps 600 years would have been more fitting for a character of such legendary status. Is Teófilo Stevenson Lawrence the most famous boxer you may never heard of, who never fought for money? Perhaps…. But now you do know him and can spread the word.
Fidel Castro commented on the news of Stevenson’s death: ‘Teófilo  Stevenson deserves the recognition of the Cuban people for his athletic success derived from his discipline, his dedication to the sport, his courage... We believe that he set a very valuable example... This young man, the humble son of a humble family... said he would not exchange his people for all the dollars in the world.’

Hycroft has a significantly larger resource package in Nevada (16.4 million ounces of gold and 562.6 million ounces of silver, M&I) plus high-grade silver zones at Brimstone and Vortex, as well as existing infrastructure. The 2026 technical study presents a 51-year scenario with a high NPV at current prices. The downside: The project is larger, more capital-intensive (initial Capex in the range of over $2 billion), not yet under construction, and without ongoing production. With a market capitalization of approximately $2.1–2.2 billion, its valuation is significantly higher than Highlander’s (approximately $1.1 billion). While Nevada is the safer jurisdiction, Peru poses political and implementation risks - however, Corani has already received approval. 

Latest Developments at Highlander (as of Summer 2026):
Acquisition of Bear Creek completed in February 2026, adding Corani and Mercedes to the portfolio. $40 million investment from Eric Sprott. Listing on the NYSE American. First exploration drilling program in a decade at Corani, involving multiple rigs. Geophysical program reveals an extensive system beneath shallow overburden. Visible construction progress is underway on-site. Mercedes is already generating revenue. Upcoming milestones: drilling results, an updated feasibility study in Q4 2026, and potential index listings.

In short: Highlander combines an approved, large-scale project already in the pre-development phase with cash flow and a high-grade secondary asset. Hycroft offers greater scale and jurisdictional quality but remains a larger, longer-term developer.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the morning of September 6, 1863, while a Union army marched on Little Rock, two Confederate generals met at fifteen paces on a plantation north of the Arkansas River and tried to kill each other. The war they were supposed to be fighting waited in the next county. Honor would not.

John S. Marmaduke was West Point steel: Missouri cavalryman, impatient, certain of his own nerve, and unwilling to serve under a man he no longer trusted. Lucius M. Walker was Tennessee-born, a planter, nephew of President Polk, ranking officer over the same cavalry, and just as certain that his name had been stained. The wound between them was not a single insult. It was a chain of slights that began at Helena on the Fourth of July, tightened at Brownsville on the twenty-fifth of August, and snapped after Bayou Meto, when Marmaduke sent for Walker on the field and Walker would not come. Marmaduke decided he would no longer take orders from him. Walker demanded to know whether he had been called a coward. Marmaduke answered like a man who knows the old code by heart: he had not used the word, but the conduct was enough. He would not serve.

The notes passed through friends. Colonel Robert Crockett—grandson of Davy Crockett—and Captain John C. Moore did what seconds so often do: they sharpened the quarrel instead of cooling it. A challenge was issued. It was accepted. Major General Sterling Price, who needed both men alive, ordered them confined to quarters. Walker never received the order. Marmaduke ignored it. At dawn they stood on Godfrey LeFevre’s ground, Colt Navy revolvers loaded in every chamber, fifteen paces of damp Arkansas earth between them.

They fired. Both missed. Marmaduke recocked and fired again. The ball struck Walker in the side, tore through kidney and spine, and dropped him paralyzed. Then came the gesture that reveals the whole age: the man who had just shot him ran forward, offered his own ambulance, and heard Walker forgive him before the sacrament. That same day Walker learned a son had been born. He died the next afternoon in Little Rock.

Price arrested Marmaduke for murder. Then he released him, because Frederick Steele’s columns were already at the door and a cavalry division could not change commanders in the face of the enemy. Four days later the capital fell. The duel had decided nothing the Union could not have decided for them.

Watch the pattern. Two men bound to one flag spent their last free hours settling a private ledger of pride while the larger war moved on. Courage without mastery of the self becomes theater. Honor without proportion becomes a luxury an army cannot afford. The river kept flowing. The city did not hold. The names remain because men would rather die right than live useful.

🇺🇸 RECLAIMING THE FUTURE 🇺🇸

PATRIOTS MUST RALLY AT THE UPCOMING MASS DEPORTATION COALITION FORUM

​For too long, we have watched Washington talk about border security while doing little to enforce the laws on the books. From unchecked illegal crossing to the strain placed on American communities, it has become abundantly clear that simple policy tweaks are no longer enough. 

To safeguard national sovereignty and restore the rule of law, America needs a clear, decisive strategy - Comprehensive border enforcement and mass interior deportation.

​This vision will take center stage in Knoxville at the upcoming Mass Deportation Coalition (MDC) Two Comma Tennessee Football Watch Party and Forum. The event promises to bring together state leaders, law enforcement veterans, and communities for a vital conversation about the future of conservative policy in Tennessee and across the nation.

​The gathering will kick off with a dedicated forum designed to bridge the gap between policy ideas and real world execution. Elected officials, conservative thought leaders, and young community members will convene for panel discussions focused on the mechanics of immigration enforcement and mass deportation.

​Rather than relying on vague political promises, these panels aim to tackle the core questions facing state and federal policy makers today - how to effectively deter unlawful entry, dismantle incentives for illegal labor, and ensure local law enforcement has the backing required to protect American communities. For young conservatives in Tennessee, the forum offers an important opportunity to help shape the future of The United States of America.
​
​A major highlight of the afternoon will feature remarks from key figures steeped in policy and border enforcement, including Mike Howell, Ryan Neuhaus, and retired Border Patrol Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino.

​Commander Bovino brings a wealth of direct operational experience. His perspective will offer attendees a grounded look at the realities of border security and the crucial role that swift removal policies play in restoring legal order. 

Speakers will address the necessity of implementing mass deportation not just as a political position, but as an essential tool to restore public safety, protect economic resources, and preserve the integrity of American citizenship.

​Building Community for the Road Ahead
​Following the policy discussions and keynote remarks, the forum will transition into a fellowship setting as attendees gather to watch the University of Tennessee Volunteers take on Arkansas.

​Events like this highlight the strength of right-wing organizing in America. By pairing serious policy debate with community fellowship, the Mass Deportation Coalition is helping build the coalition needed to drive meaningful reform. For conservatives who believe that national security begins with strong, enforced borders, this upcoming gathering in Knoxville marks an essential step forward.

#vss365 #scifisat #SpaceOpera #Iaanda01 (438 wds)
Morning After /12
The Grand Cattleier Homestead was a farmhouse in name only. Each of Pa's three daughters — the trench-coated brunette being the youngest — kept her own alabaster dome behind a pillared façade, the entire estate elaborately protected against attempts at reconnoitre.

The night before was still a blur of contrasting impressions after Iaanda had accepted the auburn-haired woman's offer of overnight hospitality: 

opulent architecture ringed by gene-modded cacti stretching to the horizon of a reclaimed dust-plain, now painstakingly watered by gangs of indentured workers who toil until the baking sun slides behind the distant hills, massaging the crops' thorns by hand to gather drops of the hallucinogenic sap that dulls the minds of the idle wealthy across the Sector.

Dinner was resplendent, served by a dozen maskless slave-servants with dead stares, hurrying to flute music from a trio of eunuchs in black togas, who seemed to be playing for their lives. 

The Grand Cattleier was gracious and witty — though Iaanda struggled to hold her backpacking-tourist cover story together under the thrust of his deft questions.

“I find it a matter of the most wonderful exoticism that an ingenuous, off-world young woman of elevated station should deem our planet free of hazard, and so journey upon it unaccompanied,” he said, eyes emotionless.

…***…
After the digestifs, she excused herself, and the brunette — den-Maanka, now in a low-cut inky dress, her ivory mask set daringly at an angle — offered to show her to her quarters, taking her elbow. 

They walked slowly through a maze of island gardens planted with scented shrubs imported from a hundred worlds at incalculable cost, the fine mist of the sprinklers moistening both young women's faces as they talked of Galactic fashion and celebrities, and den-Maanka's dreams of escaping.

Only when the doors slid shut did Iaanda realise she stood in her host's private rooms. den-Maanka let the dress slip from her shoulders and removed her mask. 

Iaanda nodded with a grin.

…***…
She sits in den-Maanka's western atrium, enjoying her morning tea and waiting for her bed-companion to join her, a part of her chiding herself for being sidetracked from finding Sorkaii — when an armoured flier banks in at high speed and the sirens begin to wail. 

A wet-haired den-Maanka arrives breathless, one hand clutching a towel at her waist. Iaanda leaps up and tackles her lover to the floor, too late.

One of the bullets meant for her has passed through den-Maanka's forehead, and she will never whisper again in the liberating darkness how she wants to be travelling on a spaceship with somebody who cares about her. Red spreads across the azure tiles and the discarded towel.

Time to sprint.

(To be continued …)

text:
I was going through some of my things and found this that I wrote on March 7, 2024. This photo was taken that same day with Zurita, one of our rescue dogs at the time. She has since been adopted, but I read these words again tonight and wanted to share them because, more than two years later, every word is still true.

“One of the most profound feelings on this plane is knowing an animal trusts you — and trusts you with its life. When you look into its eyes, you can feel with every fiber of your being the depth to which it trusts you.

To bring an animal into your life that has known suffering — true suffering — and to gain its trust is otherworldly. To take the time and practice the patience needed to heal its wounds, not just physically, but emotionally, mentally, and yes, even spiritually, is a gift.

To gain the full trust of an animal is a privilege.

The love that exists at LHRR is, in my opinion, unmatched. Every animal saved is a part of us. They each steal a piece of our hearts, and we carry them with us for the rest of our days. We work tirelessly to gain their trust and to be worthy of their transcending, unconditional love.

If you look into the eyes of an animal, it will tell you everything you need to know. You will learn its past, its fears, its insecurities, what it needs, and what makes it happy. They will bare their souls to you if you take the time to listen.

Animals are magnificent creatures, capable of holding a capacity for love that humans cannot even imagine. The way in which they trust and give themselves over to you fully is a bridge humans don’t have the capability of crossing.

As a rescuer, the best compliment I ever receive is, “I know how much you love your animals. I can feel the love between you and all of them, each and every one.”

LHRR is special in so many ways. We rescue dogs from shelters facing euthanasia. We rescue strays and medical cases. We have rescued from dog-fighting situations. We take behavioral dogs that no one else will. We offer sanctuary to those who are unadoptable. We provide rehabilitation and training. We help other rescues when they need it. We always stand behind our dogs. We have maintained a 100% save rate, and our family has expanded far beyond dogs.

But what I am most proud of — and what I believe makes us truly special — is the unbreakable bond we form with our rescues.

They truly are family. They are a part of us.

The love we share is sincere, authentic, genuine, and very real.” 

And that part has never changed.

A lot has changed since I wrote this in 2024.

We didn’t make it to Oregon. Instead, we purchased 20 acres in Texas and continued building a home and sanctuary for the animals who depend on us.

Some of the dogs I was loving when I wrote these words have since crossed the Rainbow Bridge. Their absence is felt every single day, and they will always be part of this rescue and part of me.

And since then, new dogs have come through our gates and made LHRR their home. More lives have found safety here. More animals have learned that they are loved, protected, and finally home.

The mission is still the same.

Love them. Protect them. Give them the time they need. And never give up on them.

But building and maintaining this place takes an incredible amount of money. We still have so much we need to build and improve here, while also covering food, veterinary care, utilities, housing, supplies, and the everyday bills that keep this sanctuary running.

Right now, during our birthday fundraiser, we desperately need your help.

We have a $2,500 match through the end of the day September 8th, and we still need approximately $2,200 to reach the full match.

If you are able to donate, now is such an important time. Every donation helps us keep building this place, pay our bills, buy food and treats, cover veterinary care, and continue giving every animal here the promise we made when they came through our gates:

You are safe now.
You are loved.

text:
REVIEW: Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater

How necessary was this to create? It's a question you could throw at any 'remake' whether it be film, tv, music, or videogames, and most of the time you'd probably answer it with "not really". But if it's still fun at it's core does it really matter?

Having rebuilt one of Hideo Kojima's masterpieces, Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater, from the ground up using Unreal Engine 5, Konami have created Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater, a version that treads a fine line between being a 'remake' and a 'remaster'. If I had to compare, i'd say it's more akin to The Last of Us Part 1 type of 'remake' rather than a Resident Evil  or even the Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, because structurally nothing has changed. That's not a slight on the game either, this is still Snake Eater after all, one of the greatest videogames of all time, and the origin story to one of the greatest videogame series of all time.

Operation Snake Eater:
It's not very often you play a videogame that makes you not only care about the main character, but even some of the antagonists too, yet Snake Eater achieves this with the combination of its excellent writing and timeless voice acting. The original game's cast did such an incredible job back in 2004 that Konami decided to re-use those same performances again here in Delta: Snake Eater (plus the added bonus of saving a tonne of money, of course). Hearing the likes of the iconic David Hayter (Naked Snake), Josh Keaton (Ocelot), and the incredible Lori Allen (The Boss) again is a real treat.

Imagine this, main character, CIA Agent Naked Snake, is given a covert operation by the U.S. Government, and is HALO dropped into a fictional jungle located in the Soviet Union during the Cold War in 1964. He's tasked with rescuing a Russian rocket scientist, destroying a "Treading Behemoth" capable of launching nuclear IRBM's, and defeating a superhuman unit made up of five members plus their leader. This, is Operation Snake Eater, an action packed adventure that keeps picking up pace the further you move into it, it's like you're playing a movie at times, and I mean that in the best way possible.

At the forefront of that movie-like experience is Naked Snake, an introverted guy with a passion for weaponry and the techniques that go alongside it, but as cool as Snake is, he has this seemingly impenetrable persona that's challenged multiple times by the seductive KGB spy, Eva, and even more so by his mother-like figure, The Boss. The Boss is the one who taught him everything he knows, and from the very first conversation he has with her you can hear in his voice just how highly he thinks of her. It's an extremely compelling relationship that is at the centre of the game's main themes in patriotism, family, loyalty, honor, and purpose.

Joining Snake via radio are his patriotic team members Major Zero, Para-Medic, and Sigint. A supporting cast that can be largely forgettable unless you initiate some of their optional radio calls. Para-Medic chats to Snake about classic movies after saving the game, and Sigint goes on rants about everything "weapons, equipment, and cutting-edge technology". If you aren't a fan of long talking segments in your games then these are going to be an easy skip for you because they do take you out of the gameplay loop for a good chunk of time. However, they do offer some much needed depth for these characters, it's just a case of how much you can tolerate lengthy amounts of dialogue.

The antagonists here in Snake Eater can talk a lot too, but they're written so well that you simply just sit, watch and listen, they really are that good. There's Colonel Yevgeny Borisovitch Volgin, a 6 foot 7, electricity wielding former GRU member who is the most menacing of them all, and whenever he enters a scene you almost want to stand up straight and salute him in real life. How about Revolver Ocelot? A naive gunslinging young man with an air of arrogance, loves a bit of Russian Roulette, is the leader of the Ocelot Unit, and has an obsession with Naked Snake. Let's not forget the superhuman Cobra Unit consisting of The Pain, The Fear, The End, The Fury, and The Sorrow, all of which are named after certain emotions they felt on the battlefield during World War 2. There isn't a single one of them that doesn't have something interesting about them, you'll be hard pressed to find a better bunch of antagonists in gaming.

Welcome to The Jungle:
One of the biggest changes in Delta: Snake Eater is in the control scheme, upon starting a new game you can choose to play in either "new style" or "legacy style". New style is what I chose for my full 13 hour Extreme difficulty playthrough and it features all of the new changes that are somewhat similar to Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain, whereas legacy style is supposed to mimic the original Snake Eater.

I say "supposed", because both new and legacy style use the left bumper for stalking, as well as using the triggers for aiming and shooting. In the original you could only stalk enemies using the d-pad, and the triggers were used for equipping weapons and items on-the-fly but that's now been relegated to left & right on the d-pad. These changes contradict Konami's own words though, as it clearly states in the menu that legacy style uses "the same controls as the original game", and whilst you can edit your button layout the game simply will not let you swap these two functions around. In new style these changes are perfectly fine as they suit how the game has been built this time around, but they do leave legacy style feeling redundant, with the change in camera the only compelling reason to choose it over new.

Konami's choice in trying to replicate the more fluid feel of The Phantom Pain in new style is a good idea, and for the most part they get it right. Yes, the over-the-shoulder shooting, and crouch walking do make it more fluid than the original, but there is a pretty significant downgrade in how Snake feels to control when compared to The Phantom Pain. There's a lack of precision when trying to change directions, so much so that I actually found it more precise to move him when looking through the first person view using the right bumper in some situations, and that especially rings true when he's lying in prone where it can be extremely finicky to get him to move where you want him.

Speaking of precision, the more realistic bullet drop that's been adopted here from The Phantom Pain for Snake's MK.22 Tranquilizer is an excellent addition, it's no longer near 100% accurate at all ranges, and whilst it is a controversial change, other pieces of equipment naturally become more enticing in some scenarios without forcing yourself to use them.

You most certainly won't be very accurate if you don't keep Snake's stamina bar topped up by eating the likes of fruit and wild animals. Stamina is linked to things like how quickly Snake can regenerate health, how accurate he is with his weapons, and how long he can grip onto something for. You lose stamina naturally through normal actions, but it also depletes at a faster rate if you have too many heavy weapons equipped, or, if you have an injury or ailment. Injuries and ailments also affect Snake's health bar too, and if seriously injured, like a gunshot wound or a broken bone, it shortens Snake's maximum health bar until treated in the survival viewer menu. This is one of those features that is cool as a concept but doesn't really equate to fun in-game, it's ok the first few times you get to treat Snake, but during boss fights, having to go into the menu multiple times gets a little tedious.

In the original Snake Eater you had no choice but to go into the menu's to change your camo's too. Here, Konami have acknowledged this by enabling you to equip camo's on the fly by holding up on the d-pad and using the right stick to select from presets that give you the absolute best camo index. There is a small loading screen once you've selected your camo, but it's minor in comparison to having to sift through them in the menu. This is probably my favourite feature they've added, and definitely the one I'll miss the most whenever I go back and replay the original.

Ok, so I've already told you how well written the antagonists are, but what about their boss fights? Barring one outlier, very good, they're all still brilliantly designed and still retain their hidden mechanics and little quirks. Snake Eater also has one of the best designed bosses in the series history, arguably videogame history, with there being multiple ways to defeat them that will have you wondering how on earth anyone figured it out back in 2004.

From Eating Snakes to Catching Apes:
Replayability here in Delta: Snake Eater is good with there not only being 6 difficulty options ranging from Very Easy to European Extreme, but also 28 titles to acquire by completing the game under specific requirements, some of them even rewarding you with special items to use on new game plus. The 64 Kerotan Frogs and all of the camo's from the original Snake Eater return, along with the 64 newly added very hard to find GA-KO ducks, and 15 Film Reels.

As for extra modes there are three of them, one that you have to unlock so I'm not going to spoil, another called Fox Hunt which is a multiplayer mode that is basically dead now, and the other is Snake vs. Monkey, a very simple but fun mode where you capture little apes around the various story based stages and try to set a best time. I enjoyed my time with this one, it's quite camp and is a nice change in tone from the main game, if you like arcade style game modes then you could definitely find some fun in this.

Sounds Like a Jungle, Feels Like a Jungle:
The atmosphere in Delta: Snake Eater is brilliant and every sound within the Jungle is crisp, you can hear the snakes slither through the grass, birds flutter away when startled, and even the crocodiles growling when you get too close to them, it has this melancholic ambience to it that makes it feel truly alive.

The soundtrack is still phenomenal too, from the simple tracks that play during stealth, the orchestral moments during cutscenes, to the boss fight themes. None of it is there to be background noise, it all adds to the epicness. and is the kind of music that sticks in your head long after you've finished the game, the kind where when you hear it again in a couple of years time you'll get teleported right back into the world of Snake Eater.

However, there's a new rendition of the iconic Snake Eater theme in the game's 'new' style option, it's still sung by Cynthia Harrell with no changes lyrically, but it now has a noticeable amount of auto-tune, it's definitely not terrible but the original theme definitely felt more authentic to me. The footage that plays during the Snake Eater theme has been changed in 'new style' too, it has a more James Bond-like aesthetic now and basically spoils the entire game, so I'd recommend avoiding watching it during a first playthrough.

If you want some authenticity from the visuals then play with the legacy filter on, this will ensure the game will look as close to the original as possible barring the updated graphics of course. I personally played with it off so I could see the full extent of what Konami have done visually, and when it isn't being bogged down by the "wet & shiny" look that Unreal Engine 5 can bring, Delta: Snake Eater can be a beautiful game. Character models have the most detail we've ever seen in a Metal Gear Solid game, but they often reminded me of a Madame Tussauds wax figure due to how stiff and shiny they can look at times. Environments don't suffer from this as much and is where most of the beauty in this game resides, with dense sprawling forestry, gloomy swamps, flower filled fields, snow dusted mountaintops, and even the industrial walls of Soviet-like facilities being recreated beautifully. Crawling through blades of grass and going eye-to-eye with a Milk Snake has never looked better.

A Mostly Bugless Jungle:
I had a relatively smooth experience with Delta: Snake Eater, running all high settings with DLSS Preset K set to Quality mode at 1440p on a 5700x3D & 4070 Super. I only crashed once after I ate a Gavial (Crocodile), and I only had a few stutters which surprised me given it's an Unreal Engine 5 game. The one annoying bug I had was during cutscenes where in the background it could get pretty blurry, this seemed to affect outdoor scenes more than indoor ones so I'm not sure what was causing it.

Verdict:
Despite my pretty small gripes with the game is it fun? Yes, it is absolutely fun, it's still Snake Eater at it's core. Is it necessary? If i'm being cynical, no. But to be honest, who cares? It doesn't replace the original, it sits alongside it as an alternative way to experience the Metal Gear Solid origin story, Snake Eater. If you enjoy stealth games or any other form of espionage there is a huge chance you'll love this one...

I Very Highly Recommend.

Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater is available now on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S.

text:
Army and Navy both opened their seasons today and combined to rush for 1,075 yards with 30 different ball carriers. Army beat Bryant 59-3. Navy beat Towson 42-15.

Here's why those programs are different from every other program in the country.

Last April, the Pittsburgh Steelers used a seventh round pick on a Navy running back and receiver named Eli Heidenreich.

He was in the building when they called his name. In Pittsburgh, his hometown, in front of a crowd that lost its mind.

He was wearing Full Dress Blues.

Heidenreich left Annapolis as the leading receiver in the history of the academy, with more than 3,100 yards from scrimmage, fifth most anybody has ever put up there. He graduated in May as a United States Marine Corps officer.

Every graduate owes five years of active duty.

A law passed in 2025 allows up to five graduates from each academy per year to postpone that obligation while chasing a professional sport. When the sport ends, they go back and finish it.

Heidenreich didn't just take the deferral.

He signed a ten year service contract with the Marine Corps to get it.

"I initially committed to them for five years of service afterward, but they're allowing me the opportunity to go out and pursue this football career first and give my service later. So I'm thankful for that."

"But to be able to represent them, the United States Marine Corps, the United States Navy, the military as a whole, it's an honor and something I don't take lightly."

He wasn't the only one. A teammate went at pick 226 to the Bengals, the first time in 70 years two Midshipmen were drafted in the same year.

Both were seventh round picks, where roughly one in five players ever makes a roster.

This week, both of them made the 53.

It hasn't always worked this way. In 2021 a Navy cornerback named Cameron Kinley signed with Tampa Bay as an undrafted free agent, went through rookie minicamp with the academy's permission, and then had his deferral request denied outright. He never played a down.

"I am very aware of the commitment that I made to service when I first arrived at the United States Naval Academy," Kinley wrote at the time. "However, I am deserving of the opportunity to live out another one of my life-long dreams before fulfilling my service requirement."

So when you watch Army and Navy run the football 70 times a game with sixteen different guys, understand what you're actually watching.

Nobody on either sideline is going anywhere. There's no portal, no bidding, no better offer. And the handful who do get to the NFL have to sign away more years to do it.

text:
This Humble Elevator Technician Ran Two Miles Into The World Trade Center To Save Hundreds Trapped In Stalled Elevators.

On the morning of September 11, 2001, 46-year-old elevator mechanic Charles "Chuck" Costello Jr. was working at a hotel in SoHo, twenty blocks north of the World Trade Center. It was a rare day for the New Jersey father of four to be working in Manhattan, but as a Boeing 767 slammed into the North Tower and hundreds of thousands of people began fleeing Lower Manhattan in terror, Costello did the unthinkable: he jumped out of his work site and ran over two miles straight toward the burning towers. When his coworker desperately urged him to stay back, the humble Navy veteran and devout Christian simply replied, "I'll be fine. Just keep your cellphone on," before disappearing into the thick smoke.

Inside the burning complex, stalled elevators had become horrific death traps, locking hundreds of panicked occupants inside pitch-black shafts filled with jet fuel smoke. While official contractors withdrew their crews from the chaos, Costello voluntarily charged into 1 World Trade Center to offer his technical expertise. Working alongside firefighters and police officers, who quickly came to know him as "the elevator man", he used his specialized tools and knowledge to override controls and manually force open jammed doors, freeing trapped workers line after line. After extricating countless people from the North Tower, he refused to seek safety for himself and instead ran directly into 2 World Trade Center to perform the exact same life-saving operation.

Costello’s tireless efforts saved hundreds of lives before the towers collapsed, but his refusal to abandon those trapped inside came at the ultimate price. On January 5, 2002, search and rescue crews finally recovered his remains deep beneath the rubble in a South Tower elevator shaft, resting side-by-side with a firefighter and a police officer. In his pocket were his driver’s license, union card, and rosary. Today, his son carries on his legacy as both an elevator mechanic and a volunteer firefighter. While the world remembers the overwhelming tragedy of that morning, Chuck Costello’s quiet, self-sacrificing courage stands as a testament to the highest order of human love, serving as a poignant reminder of how easily extraordinary human stories can be overlooked.

I stopped at Rupert Lowe’s claim that the boats could be stopped “virtually overnight”. In Parliament, he called for the Navy to send them back to France.

I understand the urgency. I’m furious that smugglers can make money putting people’s lives at risk. It is an absolute disgrace.

But sending people back involves another country accepting them. That is where I wanted more than a promise.

Putting Farage and Lowe’s positions side by side, I found real agreement on the aim. Lowe has also published a detailed deportation plan. Pretending he has offered nothing would be dishonest.

What impressed me about Nigel Farage was the agreement he signed with Jordan Bardella, who leads France’s National Rally. It commits their parties to a future arrangement in which Britain intercepts boats and France accepts the people returned.

That addresses a practical obstacle: what happens after interception. British crews need somewhere agreed to take people safely.

This is a pact between political parties. Both still need power, and legal and practical hurdles remain. Neither man has delivered this policy in government (a signature is a start).

Even with that limit, I’m encouraged by Farage securing a commitment from a potential French governing partner. That is work a future prime minister should be doing.

Reform’s proposed alternative is straightforward: intercept the crossings, return people to France and make the smugglers’ promised journey to Britain fail.

My verdict is that Nigel Farage and Reform UK offer the stronger leadership on this issue, because they are building the cooperation their policy would need.

text:
🚨 USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN SHOWS DRAMATIC TRANSFORMATION AFTER THAILAND CLEANUP.

LAEM CHABANG, THAILAND - The USS Abraham Lincoln drew fresh attention in Thailand after images circulated showing the aircraft carrier’s heavily rusted hull before a cleanup and its restored appearance afterward. The vessel arrived earlier this week following an unusually long deployment that kept the ship at sea for months with limited maintenance opportunities. Crews spent 286 days underway, including a stretch of more than 200 consecutive days without a full port stop, leaving the carrier streaked with rust and worn paint when it reached Laem Chabang.

The ship’s arrival offered sailors a rare break after extended operations linked to the conflict with Iran. Roughly 5,000 personnel disembarked for rest in Pattaya while maintenance teams tackled the carrier’s exterior. Rust patches along the waterline and faded coatings near the flight deck were among the most visible signs of the deployment’s toll. Navy officials described the wear as normal for a mission of this length, noting that the carrier had made only brief stops in Guam and Oman since leaving San Diego last November.

The cleanup in Thailand restored much of the ship’s appearance before it departed after a five day visit. The carrier’s escort ships, which showed similar weathering, also underwent cosmetic work during the stop. The Lincoln’s extended deployment set a modern record for consecutive days at sea, a reminder of the strain placed on crews and equipment during prolonged operations.

text:
Mike Adams: Trump’s 1980s Playbook Is Burning Down the Empire https://t.co/oSgYVn7t4N 
Why I'm Not Surprised by the Chaos in West Asia
The chaos engulfing West Asia isn't a tragic accident of diplomacy. It is the inevitable result of a decaying empire led by men whose geopolitical understanding froze somewhere around 1985. Watching President Donald Trump's administration blunder into a war with Iran, I see the same myopic arrogance that has defined American foreign policy for decades: the belief that overwhelming firepower can always force sovereign nations to submit to absurd demands.

This war never should have started. Iran did not attack the American homeland, nor did it pose an existential threat to the U.S. that justified the deployment of two carrier strike groups and thousands of tons of ordnance. Unfortunately, Trump answers to someone other than the American people -- Netanyahu, the genocidal war criminal currently in control of the Trump administration and hence the entire U.S. military.

I have watched this escalation unfold with grim recognition, because I have reported for years on Washington's addiction to military force and its inability to learn from history. Iran, unlike the weak, fractured states America bulldozed in Iraq and Afghanistan, has studied American tactics and built a strategy of resilience. As one analysis put it, the United States launched an attack "with boasts of swift victory" but instead "ignited a resilient Iranian counter-punch that has rewritten the rules of modern warfare" [1]. This conflict has revealed that America is a declining power which can no longer project force at will, and Iran has proven it [2].

The administration, still trapped in its 1980s mindset, believes it can bully Tehran into submission with a few bombing raids. Yet every escalation -- the assassinations, the economic strangulation, the belligerent talk -- has only galvanized Iranian resistance. As I have stated in my own broadcasts, this is not a path to victory; it is a march toward catastrophic defeat.

The Escalation Trap: Why Trump Can't Stop Digging
President Trump has fallen into the oldest trap in warfare: he cannot stop digging because he cannot afford to admit he is trapped. This is the escalation dynamic familiar to any student of imperial decline. His advisors, many of whom possess an abysmal ignorance of history, tell him that one more blow will break the enemy's will. They fundamentally misunderstand the resilience of the Persian, Russian, and Chinese peoples -- cultures that have survived countless invasions and foreign interventions, only to outlast their conquerors.

Every tactic the U.S. has tried has failed. Economic sanctions intended to cripple Iran have instead forged closer ties between Tehran, Moscow, and Beijing, who signed a 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty to counterbalance Western influence . Bombings have killed high-ranking officials like Ali Larijani, but they have also steeled the Iranian public's resolve [3]. The assassination campaign has eliminated commanders, yet the Iranian military has proven its capacity to strike back, inflicting hundreds of U.S. casualties and successfully threatening vital chokepoints [4].

Meanwhile, the United States is depleting its own store of power. The American public is losing its appetite for a forever war, especially as inflation and diesel shortages bite at home. The military is running low on the smart munitions necessary for modern warfare, and domestic support is sagging as the midterm elections approach. Each new strike is a gamble that risks a wider regional conflagration -- yet the administration projects an image of decisive leadership.

As I stated in a recent broadcast, the war is not just unwinnable; it is already lost [2]. We have exhausted our credibility, our treasury, and our patience, and we have nothing to show for it but a burning region and a hardened global alliance against us.

NATO and Europe: The Real Victims of American Empire
While Washington's war machine has focused its fury on Iran, the true casualties of this 1980s adventure may well be the transatlantic alliance itself. Europe has been dragged into a conflict that threatens its economic future, and its leaders have dutifully taken the hit. The U.S. war economy relies on a weak Europe, one that is dependent on American energy and patronage. It was no accident that the Nord Stream pipelines, Europe's key to energy independence from both Russia and the U.S., were sabotaged. This was "economic warfare against allies," a blunt instrument used to cripple Europe's industrial base and ensure its continued subservience to American interests [5].

European leaders, tragically, have been complicit in their own hobbling. Rather than assert their strategic autonomy, they have followed Washington's lead, prepared to sacrifice their economies and endure the freezing winters of a scorched-earth energy war. I have argued that they are not strategic thinkers; they are administrators of a slowly disintegrating empire, unable to see that their long-term interests diverge from the globalist agenda peddled in D.C. [6].

The cracks in NATO are no longer hairline fractures. Turkey has demonstrated its willingness to pursue its own interests, flatly refusing to be a pawn against Iran or Russia. The U.S. has also found itself abandoned by its allies when it needed support, as evidenced by Trump's furious blast at NATO nations over their refusal to deploy warships to the Strait of Hormuz [7]. The Atlanticist project is now vaporware. Why would European soldiers die for an American empire that views them as expendable vassals? The alliance's structure persists, but its spirit is long gone, and the United States itself is rapidly becoming the empire's gravedigger.

GCC Countries: Targets, Not Partners
The Gulf Cooperation Council monarchies are learning a bitter lesson in 2026: they are targets, not partners. American military bases, emblems of the so-called security guarantee, have transformed nations like Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE into primary targets for Iranian retaliation. Their elaborate defense systems have proved woefully inadequate against the swarm tactics of hypersonic drones and ballistic missiles. These states are bleeding billions in defense spending while their critical energy facilities are vulnerable to fire, turning their wealth into a liability.

The conflict has also hammered their export capacity. Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused a huge drop in energy shipments, with key Gulf facilities like Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery damaged by missile strikes [8]. Qatar's precious LNG wealth, a cornerstone of its national power, is also on the line. Damage to these facilities will take years, not months, to repair -- and every escalation delays that recovery.

This economic devastation is not an accident; it is part of a broader strategy that has exhausted the GCC's financial war chest. I noted with particular interest the reporting from last year that detailed how Saudi Arabia sent signals about fiscal stress and the crumbling petrodollar system, with demands for trillions in security guarantees illustrating the sheer weight of imperial protection rackets [9].

Washington extracts tribute while offering only hollow promises and making its vassals targets. The deal offered by the U.S. empire is becoming so obviously one-sided that even the Gulf monarchies, so often slow to read the writing on the wall, are beginning to look for exits.

The Strait of Hormuz Is the World's Lifeline -- and We're Cutting It
The true insanity of this conflict is on display in the waters of the Strait of Hormuz. This is not just a regional dispute over territorial integrity; this is the world's principal economic chokepoint, responsible for carrying about 20% of global oil and one-third of the world's LNG [8]. Yet, much more is at stake. The global food system depends on Persian Gulf outflows of helium, sulfur, fertilizers, and petrochemicals that are the invisible inputs to modern agriculture and industry [10]. Iran's closure of the strait was not an idle threat; it was an act of economic defiance that instantly caused global energy prices to surge and sent supply chains into chaos [11].

Blockades are one thing; but a prolonged closure is turning into a catastrophe of unimaginable proportions. The damage to Qatar's LNG facilities alone will take an estimated three to five years to repair [12]. If the conflict continues and the disruption stretches into a lost decade, the world will face a famine unlike anything in modern history. Global starvation would not be a poetic metaphor but a daily reality as fertilizer and grain shipments grind to a halt [10]. It is a reckoning that would make the Great Depression look like a downturn in a business cycle.

This is not a prophecy of doom; it is basic arithmetic. The U.S. has chosen to cut its own throat and the throat of the global economy by treating the world's most critical supply line as a medium for political gamesmanship.

A New World Order Is Rising: China, Russia, and the Reckoning
Out of the ashes of the American empire in West Asia, a new world order is being born. Iran's successful defiance is more than a military turning point; it is a powerful psychological symbol proving that nations can stand up to the United States and survive. When Washington's primary tools are sanctions and violence, and those tools fail, the myth of the indispensable nation collapses with them. As I have said, Iran's resilience is a testament to the reality that "nations no longer must bow to the U.S. empire" if they are willing to pay the price for their freedom [13].

This new order is being built by China and Russia, not through threats, but through alternative structures of trade and cooperation. They are actively constructing overland and maritime corridors, like China's Belt and Road Initiative and the nascent Russia-Iran North-South corridor, to bypass the chokepoints controlled by the U.S. Navy. Their accords, like the 20-year pact between Russia and Iran, provide mutual defense that offers a shield against U.S. coercion [14].

The crumbling of American influence is most visible in its own inability to compete on the domestic front. The U.S. cannot even power its own AI ambitions, let alone project power to maintain a unipolar world. While Washington is mired in a 1980s worldview and protectionist trade wars, rival nations are advancing. Trump's tariffs are not protecting America; they are an "embargo against America," raising costs for its own consumers and forcing its companies to innovate in a vacuum, disconnected from global supply chains. This economic self-sabotage while our rivals collaborate is the clearest sign yet that we are headed for a historic decline.

The Reckoning Is Here: Time to Face Reality
The reckoning we face is not in the distant future; it is arriving right now. I see no evidence of learning in Washington, only a deepening delusion that defines the Pentagon's strategic planning. I have interviewed many experts, from whistleblowers to military veterans, and the consensus is that the empire is in its final, frantic phase. We have invested trillions in weapons designed to demolish other nations, yet our own bridges are crumbling, our people are chronically sick (and obese), and our economy is hollowed out. The enemies are not gathering on our shores; they are feasting on our ruin from within.

The American people are the ones suffering from these policies. This war is not hurting the globalists who orchestrated it; it is hurting the everyday American who is coping with the diesel shortages, grocery inflation, and the constant drumbeat of fear. We are not just fighting a foreign enemy; we are fighting ourselves, and we are losing.

We are now confronted with a choice: to continue this delusional path toward national ruin, or to begin the painful process of constructing a new society that prioritizes liberty, self-reliance, and life. I believe we must extricate ourselves from this war and finally acknowledge that we are not, and never had the right to be, the world's policeman. We are no longer the essential nation, and our attempts to prove otherwise are literally burning down the world.

We need to rebuild America with honesty, dignity and a deep cleansing of corruption, incompetence and financial influence to restore America to something resembling its founding vision. Until we do that, the slow, grinding, insufferable collapse will be painful and catastrophic.

We the American people deserve better than this.
