text:
# 🏈 Commanders @ Eagles — The Catch-Up

Philadelphia allowed one touchdown to wide receivers on 151 throws under ten yards last season. One. Washington allowed 18 touchdowns on 249 of the same throws, then went out and signed three receivers who live there.

Dallas Goedert caught 9 passes inside the 10-yard line last year and 8 of them were touchdowns. He is +230.

> Sunday, Sept 13 · 4:25 PM ET · Lincoln Financial Field, Philadelphia · outdoors, 81 degrees, 10 mph wind
> Eagles −5.5 (DraftKings −4.5) · Total 44.5 (DraftKings 45.5) · Commanders +180 / Eagles −218
> Dan Quinn vs. Nick Sirianni · division game

---

## Part 1: What you missed

**Philadelphia.** A.J. Brown is a Patriot. That is 115 targets and 33% of the Eagles' air yards gone. Jahan Dotson went to Atlanta. The replacements are Dontayvion Wicks (Green Bay), Hollywood Brown (Kansas City), Elijah Moore and rookie Makai Lemon. DeVonta Smith is the number one now. Goedert is the tight end; Grant Calcaterra is on reserve. Saquon Barkley is back at 29, with Tank Bigsby (from Jacksonville) and Will Shipley behind him. Riq Woolen came from Seattle to play corner. Hurts is Hurts.

**Washington.** Deebo Samuel is a 49er, Zach Ertz is on reserve, Brian Robinson is a Falcon, Chris Rodriguez is a Jaguar. That is the entire 2025 red zone: 20 red-zone targets and 11 touchdowns' worth of production gone. In: **Stefon Diggs** (New England), **Chig Okonkwo** (Tennessee), Rachaad White (Tampa), Treylon Burks, Jerome Ford, Dyami Brown. Terry McLaurin is back after a 9-game season. Jayden Daniels played 7 games last year; Marcus Mariota played the other 7 and was better by the numbers. Jacory Croskey-Merritt is the lead back.

One sentence: Philadelphia lost a receiver, Washington lost its whole end zone and bought a new one that does not fit.

---

## Part 2: The line, translated

**Eagles −5.5** (−4.5 at DraftKings). Bet Philadelphia, win by 6 (or 5 at DK). Bet Washington, lose by 5 or fewer (or 4). Shop it: −4.5 is a full point better for Eagles backers.

**Total 44.5** (45.5 at DK) implies **Commanders 19.5, Eagles 25**.

**+180 / −218.** About 36% Washington, 69% Philadelphia.

Prop prices: **+230** means the book thinks 30%. Goedert scored in 53% of his games. **−135** means 57%. Barkley scored in 50% and had one touchdown on 15 carries inside the 5.

---

## Part 3: Two words you need today

**Short zone.** Throws under ten air yards. Most offenses live there. Some defenses let you complete them and then tackle; a few let you complete them and then walk into the end zone. Philadelphia is the first kind. Washington is the second.

**Tush push.** Philadelphia's quarterback sneak with two players pushing from behind. It is why Jalen Hurts took 11 carries inside the 5 last year and scored 5 times, and why Barkley took 15 and scored once. The goal line in Philadelphia belongs to the quarterback.

---

## Part 4: The whiteboards

**Philadelphia's defense** lets you throw short and gives you nothing for it. Receipt: 198.2 passing yards allowed, eighth-fewest. 29.6 to tight ends, fewest in the league. Sack rate 6.7%.

| Philadelphia, throws faced 2025 | Throws | Caught | TDs | Worth to offense |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Behind the line | 101 | 65% | 0 | −0.35 |
| 0 to 9 yards | 256 | 68% | 6 | −0.06 |
| 10 to 19 yards | 109 | 44% | 3 | +0.24 |
| 20 or more | 72 | 29% | 5 | +0.30 |

Wide receivers on short throws: 151 targets, 849 yards, **one touchdown**. Tight ends on short throws: 57 targets, 273 yards, −0.20 per throw. The one place Philadelphia bends is deep, where they let you complete 29%.

**Washington's defense** is the photographic negative. Receipt: 254.5 passing yards allowed, third-most. 107.0 rushing yards to backs, second-most. 150.3 to receivers, fourth-most.

| Washington, throws faced 2025 | Throws | Caught | TDs | Worth to offense |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 to 9 yards | 249 | 73% | **18** | +0.37 |
| 10 to 19 yards | 136 | 56% | 10 | +0.41 |
| 20 or more | 55 | 38% | 5 | +0.67 |

Tight ends against Washington: 7 touchdowns on 67 short throws, 4 more on 23 intermediate throws worth **+1.40 each**, the most expensive band any defense allowed to any position. Goedert's 7.2-yard routes are in the first. His seam routes are in the second.

**The coaches.** Same two coaches, same two systems. Philadelphia's caveat is a rebuilt secondary (Woolen, Jonathan Jones, Michael Carter II); the front seven that produced the short-zone suppression is intact. Washington's caveat is the quarterback: Daniels' 7 games were worse than Mariota's 7 by completion rate above expectation (−3.3 to +5.0). Nobody prices that.

---

## Part 5: The prop board

### Dallas Goedert · TE · Eagles

- **Who:** Philadelphia's red zone, by himself.
- **What he does:** 7.2-yard routes, 3.61 separation. Inside the 10 last year: 9 targets, 8 touchdowns. Red zone overall: 15 targets, 10 touchdowns.
- **Last year (15 games):** 39.4 yards, median 32. Over 34.5 in 6 of 15. Scored in **8 of 15**, including his last three.
- **The book says:** 34.5 receiving yards. Over 3.5 receptions −103. Anytime TD **+230**.
- **The play:** **Anytime TD at +230.** A 53% scorer at a 30% price, against a defense that gave up 11 touchdowns to tight ends, and A.J. Brown's 13 red-zone targets need a new home. The yards are a coin flip; skip them.

### Saquon Barkley · RB · Eagles

- **Who:** Last year's rushing champion runner-up, now 29.
- **Last year (16 games):** 71.3 rushing yards, **median 60**. Over 75.5 in 6 of 16, but 122, 78, 132, 68 in his last four (the 132 was against Washington). Inside the 5: 15 carries, **1 touchdown**. Catches in his last five games: 0, 0, 2, 0, 0.
- **The book says:** 75.5 rushing (76.5 at one book). 18.5 carries. Over 2.5 receptions −103. 15.5 receiving yards. Anytime TD **−135**.
- **The play:** **Under 2.5 receptions at −125 and Under 15.5 receiving yards.** He stopped catching passes in November. **Fade the touchdown at −135:** the book says 57%, he scored in 50%, and the goal line is Hurts' (5 of 11 inside the 5 to Barkley's 1 of 15). The rushing yards are a lean Over on the finish and the matchup (Washington allowed 107 a game to backs), but it is a lean, not a hammer: 6 of 16.

### Jalen Hurts · QB · Eagles

- **Who:** The quarterback whose value is at the goal line. 11 carries inside the 5, 5 touchdowns.
- **What he does:** 8.9-yard routes, 17% into tight windows, 28 throws a game.
- **Last year (16 games):** 201.5 passing yards, median 184. Two or more touchdown passes in **8 of 16**. Rushing 26.3 a game, median 29. Scored a rushing touchdown in 6 of 16.
- **The book says:** 210.5 passing yards (214.5 at FanDuel). Over 1.5 passing TDs **+110**. 27.5 rushing. Anytime TD +126.
- **The play:** **Over 1.5 passing TDs at +110.** He did it exactly half the time at a 48% price, and Washington allowed 18 short-zone touchdowns, the exact throw Hurts makes inside the 20. The rushing touchdown at +126 (38% actual, 44% implied) is a pass.

### Stefon Diggs · WR · Commanders

- **Who:** 32, new team, coming off 809 yards in 10 games for New England.
- **What he does:** 8.9-yard routes, 2.98 separation, 83% catch rate, +1.04 yards after catch over expected. A short, sure-handed possession receiver.
- **Last year (17 logged games):** 59.6 yards, **median 43**. Over 41.5 in 9 of 17, last five 66.8. Four or more catches in 9 of 17. Scored in 4 of 17.
- **The book says:** 41.5 receiving yards (40.5 to 42.5). Over 3.5 receptions −135. Anytime TD +355.
- **The play:** **Over 41.5, lightly.** Nine of seventeen with a hot finish, and Philadelphia allows the completion at 68%. **Fade the touchdown at any price:** one receiver touchdown allowed on 151 short throws, and his 8.9-yard route is a short throw.

### Jacory Croskey-Merritt · RB · Commanders

- **Who:** Washington's lead back, in a room that lost its goal-line finisher.
- **Last year (15 logged games):** 45.3 rushing yards, median 32. Over 40.5 in 5 of 15. Scored in **6 of 17**. Inside the 10: 21 carries, 5 touchdowns. Inside the 5: 13 and 3.
- **The book says:** 40.5 rushing yards. 11.5 carries. Anytime TD **+141**.
- **The play:** **Anytime TD at +141.** A 35% scorer at a 41% price looks fair until you remember Rodriguez (14 carries inside the 5, 5 touchdowns) is gone and White (0 for 10 on red-zone targets in Tampa) is not that guy. The yards are a coin flip against a defense that allowed 91.5 a game to backs.

### Terry McLaurin · WR · Commanders

- **Who:** The deep threat, back from a 9-game year.
- **What he does:** 14-yard routes, the deepest in the game, into a defense that completed 44% at 10 to 19 and 29% past 20.
- **Last year (9 games):** 58.3 yards, median 54. Over 51.5 in 6 of 9. Four or more catches in **3 of 9**. Scored in 3 of 10.
- **The book says:** 51.5 receiving yards (52.5 at two books). Over 3.5 receptions −133 (4.5 at some). Anytime TD +251.
- **The play:** **Under 3.5 receptions at +104.** Six of nine games with three or fewer catches. His yards come in one or two chunks or not at all, and Philadelphia's deep coverage is where chunks go to die. The yardage Under is the same idea with more variance.

### DeVonta Smith · WR · Eagles

- **Who:** The number one now. 12.1-yard routes, 2.86 separation.
- **Last year (16 games):** 59.8 yards, median 49.5. Over 66.5 in 5 of 16, last five 40.4. Six or more catches in 6 of 16. Scored in 4 of 16.
- **The book says:** 66.5 receiving yards (64.5 at one book). Over 5.5 receptions +108. Anytime TD +182.
- **The play:** **Pass on the yards, lean the touchdown.** The line already moved up 7 yards to price Brown's departure. His last five were 42, 37, 50, 42, 25. But Washington allowed 8 receiver touchdowns on short throws and 5 more at 10 to 19, and Smith is now the only receiver Hurts trusts. +182 for a 25% scorer stepping into 33% of the team's air yards is a dart.

---

## Part 6: Between the lines

**Washington bought the perfect Ertz replacement and walked him into the one defense that erases his job.** Chig Okonkwo: 3.9-yard routes, 3.77 separation, +1.78 yards after catch over expected, an excellent short-area tight end. Philadelphia against tight ends on short throws: 57 targets, 273 yards, 3 touchdowns, −0.20 per throw. His only yardage line is 27.5 at one book. Under it, and fade the touchdown at +443.

**The whole Washington haul is short-area talent walking into the best short-area defense in football.** Diggs (8.9-yard routes), Okonkwo (3.9), White (a checkdown back). The one Commander built to attack where Philadelphia is soft, McLaurin at 14 yards, is the one with 2.38 separation drawing Quinyon Mitchell. That is not a talent problem. It is a fit problem, and fit does not show up in yards-allowed tables.

**Dontayvion Wicks at +316 is a fade, not a dart.** Scored once in 13 games. The market has priced Brown's vacated snaps onto him at 24%. Nothing in his file supports it.

**Barkley's goal line was never his.** Fifteen carries inside the 5, one score. Hurts, 11 and 5. The market prices Barkley at −135 to score anyway because he is Saquon Barkley. His 8 touchdowns in 16 games mostly came from distance, which is fine, and it is not a 57% proposition.

---

## Part 7: How Sunday probably goes

Philadelphia does what the numbers say: eleven plays, seven runs, Goedert on a first-read RPO for 14, a field goal. Washington's best drive is Daniels escaping for 16 and Diggs on a shallow cross for 19; it dies at the 18 on two throws inside the 10 to a room without Deebo or Ertz. 3–3. The heat starts telling on Washington's front, Philadelphia runs 14 plays, and Hurts finds Goedert from 7 on a rub out of a bunch. 13–3 at the half after an Elliott field goal.

Quinn's adjustment (more play-action, McLaurin on crossers) produces a touchdown to Diggs from 12 on third-and-goal. Then Barkley on six of eight plays, Hurts sneaks from the 1, and Goedert again from 11 with Nick Cross a step late.

> **Eagles 27, Commanders 16.** Total 43, just under. Washington crosses the 30 four times and kicks three.

---

## Part 8: The plays

**Dallas Goedert anytime TD (+230).** Eight of 15; 8 of 9 inside the 10.

**Over Jalen Hurts 1.5 passing TDs (+110).** Eight of 16; Washington allowed 18 short-zone touchdowns.

**Under Saquon Barkley 2.5 receptions (−125).** Zero catches in four of his last five games.

**Jacory Croskey-Merritt anytime TD (+141).** Six of 17, and the goal-line competition left.

**Under Terry McLaurin 3.5 receptions (+104).** Three of 9 over.

**Over Stefon Diggs 41.5 receiving yards (−114), lightly.** Nine of 17, last five 67.

Darts: DeVonta Smith anytime TD +182. Goedert 2+ touchdowns (ask your book). Drew Stevens Over 6.5 kicking points if offered: Washington moves it and stops at the 25.

Fades: Barkley anytime TD −135 (1 of 15 inside the 5). Diggs anytime TD +355 (one receiver touchdown allowed on 151 short throws). Wicks anytime TD +316 (1 of 13). Okonkwo Under 27.5 receiving yards (one book) and fade his touchdown.

Game: Eagles −4.5 at DraftKings. Under 44.5, light.

The stack: Hurts Over 1.5 passing TDs + Goedert anytime TD + Barkley Under 2.5 receptions. One story: the favorite scores through the air in the short area, the tight end finishes, and the running back is a runner.

---

## Part 9: What to watch

Watch Washington's first trip inside the 20. If the throws go to Diggs and Okonkwo underneath, that is 208 short throws last year that produced 4 touchdowns against this defense, and the Under on Washington's team total is on. If Quinn dials McLaurin on a deep post, he read the same table you did.

Then watch Philadelphia's first snap inside the 5. It will be a sneak. Barkley's −135 is priced as if it might not be.

Two teams split last season. One lost its entire red zone in the offseason, the other lost a 1,000-yard receiver and still gets to attack the softest nine yards in football. Which matters more in Week 1, Washington's new talent or the fact that almost none of it fits?

Repost if this got a friend caught up before the late window.

The Read: I lean toward the Toronto Blue Jays (ML -123).

The Fundamentals:
Two days ago, I backed Kansas City in this series based on a pitching advantage that didn't pan out. Today, the structural logic points the other way, and I am backing the Blue Jays to exploit a vulnerable starter.

The Royals are sending Randy Dobnak, a contact-heavy pitcher with a small sample size (just 40 strikeouts in 57.2 innings) who allows significant traffic (1.39 WHIP, .258 opponent average). The Blue Jays counter with Spencer Arrighetti, who despite a higher ERA, boasts a much stronger strikeout profile (97K in 99 IP) and a better WHIP (1.34). In 95-degree heat, balls in play carry further, making a contact-heavy pitcher like Dobnak highly vulnerable. Our track record shows that fading small-sample, contact-heavy pitchers is a highly reliable edge. I make Toronto's true win probability around 58%.

Market Pricing & Execution:
The sportsbook has Toronto priced as road favorites at -123, which carries a de-vigged fair probability of 52.7%. Polymarket currently has the Blue Jays to win priced at 53¢. (I wasn't able to isolate today's specific game on Kalshi).

With my read at 58%, there is a solid ~5-point edge on Toronto's fair value. My calibration data shows that trusting these larger (5+ point) edge calculations when we disagree with the market has been our most actionable and profitable strategy (26-16 on resolved calls). 

For execution, Polymarket offers a better number. The sportsbook's -123 moneyline requires a 55.1% raw break-even, while Polymarket offers the Blue Jays at 53¢ (53% break-even). The best execution is taking Toronto YES at 53¢ on Polymarket.

Parents? We don't need no stinking parents!'
===========
“If any staff member learns a student is transgender or gender non-conforming,” the document says, according to the lawsuit, “that information should be relayed to the school principal without delay.” The principal can discuss accommodations and schedule a meeting to go over pronouns and locker rooms. If the student doesn’t want to tell the parents, “that request will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis,” factoring in age, grade, welfare, “and any other relevant information.”

The Justice Department argues this violates two federal laws: First, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, which requires schools to respect the ability of parents “to inspect and review the education records of their children.” Second, the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment, which requires parental consent before a student submits to a “survey, analysis, or evaluation” on sensitive topics, including “sex behavior or attitudes.”

If the Justice Department has the authority to go after these bad policies, it could take some of the litigation burden from busy parents, who might not realize what schools are doing or the importance of objecting in advance. In the case that reached the Supreme Court, Mirabelli v. Bonta, one set of parents said they didn’t know that their daughter had changed genders at school until she attempted suicide.

The Kansas City district has denied breaking the law, and in a letter to the government last month, it offered a narrow interpretation of deception as a rare exception. “There are very few limited circumstances where a school district might, depending on the circumstances, not be able to notify the student’s parents,” it said, including if the student has already turned 18 or if there’s an active investigation into “abuse or neglect by the parent.”

That’s far more constrained than “a case-by-case basis.” The district also said in its letter that the guidance document “fully anticipates the participation of a student’s parents in seeking to support a transgender or gender non-conforming student’s needs within the school environment.”

And what about nonabusive parents who oppose a transition? The lawsuits will keep coming until the judiciary makes clear that school administrators can’t"

text:
On this day in 1781, the most infamous traitor in American history led a British force into the heart of his own home state, burned a town nearly to the ground, and watched as his men slaughtered a surrendering American garrison. The traitor's name was Benedict Arnold, and this was the last thing he ever did on American soil.

By now Arnold was no longer a secret turncoat. His treason had been exposed the year before, he had fled to the British, and they had made him a general in a red coat. He was born and raised in Connecticut. New London, the target, was a busy privateering port only a few miles from his birthplace. He knew this coast, these towns, these people. And he came to burn them.

On September 6, Arnold split his force in two. One column, under his command, moved on New London itself, and soon much of the town was in flames, warehouses, ships, homes, one of the worst burnings of the entire war. But the true horror unfolded across the river, at a small earthwork called Fort Griswold, held by roughly 150 Connecticut militiamen under Colonel William Ledyard.

The British column stormed the fort. The defenders fought hard and inflicted heavy casualties on the attackers before they were overwhelmed. And then, with the fighting essentially over and resistance collapsing, came the atrocity. According to the American accounts that came down, when the British broke in and Colonel Ledyard offered his surrender, a British officer took Ledyard's own surrendered sword and ran him through with it, killing the commander in the act of giving up. What followed was a massacre. Enemy soldiers bayoneted and shot down militiamen who had thrown down their arms, killing scores of men after the fort had fallen. Of the garrison, the great majority were killed or wounded, many of them after the surrender.

It was the kind of butchery that seared itself into memory, an American town in flames and its surrendering sons cut down, all of it under the direction of a man who had once been one of the greatest heroes of the very cause he was now burning. There is a bitter symmetry that historians have never gotten over. Years earlier, Benedict Arnold had been a brilliant, brave American general, wounded in the leg leading charges that helped win the pivotal victory at Saratoga. He had done as much as almost anyone to win the war. And here he was, on his home ground, presiding over the murder of his own countrymen.

The raid did little to change the course of the war, which was already rushing toward its end. In fact, while Arnold was burning New London, the real decision was being made far to the south, where a French fleet had just sealed off the Chesapeake and doomed Cornwallis at Yorktown. Arnold's raid was a cruel, pointless act of destruction at the very moment his new masters were losing.

And it was his farewell. Not long after, Arnold sailed for England, and he never set foot in America again. His last act on American soil was to burn a Connecticut town and stand by as its defenders were massacred. He lived out his years in Britain, distrusted even by the people he had betrayed his country to join, and died there, his name transformed forever from that of a hero into the American word for traitor. Fort Griswold is where he wrote the final, ugliest line of that story.

Wright explained that the Trump administration rewrote refinery specifications so American plants could squeeze 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐥 out of the same barrel of crude. New York, Connecticut, California and other Democrat-run states declined to adopt the change — a choice Wright said only makes sense if the goal is higher prices, not lower ones.

The squeeze isn’t just domestic. text:
In the tense summer of 1776, as British warships crowded New York Harbor after the Battle of Long Island, inventor David Bushnell of Connecticut offered the Continental Army a startling new weapon: a hand-cranked, oak-and-iron submersible called the Turtle. Built to slip unseen beneath an enemy hull and plant a timed explosive, the one-man craft was entrusted to Sergeant Ezra Lee of the Connecticut Line. Shortly after midnight on September 6, Lee entered the cramped vessel, sealed its hatch, and began the laborious two-hour journey against strong tides toward Admiral Richard Howe's flagship, HMS Eagle.

Once beneath the sixty-four-gun warship, Lee attempted to bore into the hull with the Turtle's screw-like auger so he could attach the powder magazine. Copper sheathing on the Eagle's bottom defeated the tool; the compass inside the dark, leaking cabin failed; and the incoming tide threatened to carry him into daylight and discovery. After several fruitless tries, Lee abandoned the effort, surfaced, and released the explosive charge. The keg drifted away and later detonated harmlessly on the surface, startling British lookouts but doing no damage.

Though the mission failed to sink its target, the Turtle's sortie marked the first recorded submarine attack in history and revealed both the ingenuity and the limits of early underwater warfare. British officers thereafter regarded every floating object with suspicion, while American leaders gained a glimpse of technologies that would one day transform naval combat. Lee returned safely, towed in by a whaleboat, having proved that a determined crew in a primitive submersible could at least reach the most powerful ship in the harbor and live to tell of it.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the morning of September 6, 1781, the traitor came home.

Benedict Arnold had once been the most daring officer in the Continental Army—the man who dragged cannon through the Maine wilderness, who held the line at Saratoga while others hesitated, who understood that war is decided not by numbers but by the will to strike first and strike where it hurts. Ambition had consumed him. Feeling slighted, unpaid, and unappreciated, he sold himself to the British and received in return a brigadier’s commission and the chance to prove he was still a soldier of consequence. Sir Henry Clinton handed him the knife and pointed it at Connecticut.

New London was a nest of privateers, a harbor that bled British shipping. It was also, cruelly, Arnold’s own country. He had grown up just upriver in Norwich. Now he returned not as a son but as an instrument of power. Thirty-two ships carried seventeen hundred British, Hessian, and Loyalist troops. The wind delayed them until daylight. Lookouts at Fort Griswold fired the alarm. Arnold split his force like a man who knew the ground too well: he took the western bank himself and marched on New London and the weaker Fort Trumbull; Lieutenant Colonel Edmund Eyre took eight hundred men against Fort Griswold on the Groton Heights.

Fort Trumbull fell after a single volley. Its small garrison spiked the guns and rowed across the Thames to die with their brothers. New London burned. Warehouses, wharves, ships, shops, and homes went up in sheets of flame. The Hannah exploded and flung fire farther into the town. Arnold watched the place of his youth consume itself and called it strategy.

Across the river the real contest unfolded. Colonel William Ledyard held Fort Griswold with roughly one hundred fifty militiamen—farmers, sailors, and townsmen who had hours, not days, to prepare. They refused the first demand to surrender. They threw back the first assault. Eyre fell mortally wounded. Major Montgomery was killed as he mounted the parapet. For forty minutes a handful of amateurs bled a professional force. Then the British poured over the walls.

What followed has never been settled in the minds of those who study power. Ledyard offered his sword in surrender. An officer—accounts name a Loyalist major—took it and drove it through him. The garrison, already beaten, was cut down. Eighty-five Americans lay dead inside the fort; most of the rest were wounded, many mortally. Arnold later reported the British lost forty-eight killed and one hundred forty-five wounded—proof that even a traitor’s victory can be expensive when the defenders refuse to play their assigned role.

The raid succeeded in its immediate object. New London smoldered. Ships that could not flee upriver were destroyed. Clinton received a report of “spirited conduct.” Yet the larger game had already moved south. Washington and Rochambeau were marching toward Yorktown. Arnold’s fire on the Thames changed nothing about the war’s end. It only revealed the man: a brilliant tactician who could not master the one force that always outlasts talent—reputation. He had wanted respect from his new masters. He received instead a footnote of ash and a massacre that Connecticut never forgot.

Power is rarely clean. The man who burns his own country to prove he still matters discovers that the flames remember his name longer than his victories do.

Aw, man!  the long post above was an off-the-cuff response at about 1:30 a.m., when I was listening to the end of The Enforcer's war news podcast.  (And of course South Africa was selected as the case study to get under Elon's skin a bit. 😁)  There are way too many bits of information missing in my post, which I skipped because it was already too much like cranking out a term paper when I was half asleep.  Could barely keep my eyes open, actually.  I think the main question people might have is why I mentioned mining as an issue in a national uprising/revolution, and that's because of the abject working conditions.  It was another thing mentioned a lot on the news in the US -- people dying from mining accidents, and those who survived remained working in scary conditions.  Not just slave-like, because owners wanted their slaves/investments to survive.  Mining was an industry that treated its workers as expendable.  That was a part of the uprising -- the exploitation of the workers combined with the wealth of the owners.  The workers weren't reading propaganda, or anything at all.  They were working.  They were treated as though their lives were worthless.  The people sending them into those conditions took most of the value derived from their work and shared little risk.  This is a part of why mining was important in making people willing to rebel.  There's usually a very good reason when people rebel anywhere.

A side story -- one of my professors in college (a man who'd served in the Air Force and specialized in African history, married to a lady from Grenada who taught at Howard U. for a long time) once knew a pilot who flew a white family out of an African country when things were going south there -- might have been Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe).  They offered him a little bag of diamonds as payment.  He didn't think that they could possibly be real, and he'd never been paid that way before, but he took pity and flew them out of the chaos.  Many years later when he needed money, he thought of that little bag of "diamonds" in his dresser drawer, and decided to see if they were worth anything.  Yes they were real, and as he found out, worth about $60k.  These days that sounds like money to maybe buy a Tesla, but back then, 60k would buy you a 4-bedroom house in the suburbs, and probably a new car, too.

I know that Elon's father supposedly owned a stake in an emerald mine.  (Ugh, gotta google that guy again to get my facts straight...)  That was in Zambia, and again involved aviation -- he traded his airplane for it.  I don't think that he personally had to witness the mining conditions, though.  If he had, that could have contributed to his "psychological issues."  And he eventually lost his share of the mine, but I'd rely on a google search to tell me why, so I'm not covering that here.  

The real screwed-up stuff was happening with the police, as I mentioned.  This is why it was lower priority to mention the mines.  South African police were beating up black kids, and a few would die, just about every day.  Even Steve Biko was beaten to death (you can google him), which outraged Americans following events there.  

Another omission -- It wasn't just one way.  There was resistance.  There were attacks on police but mostly attacks among the resistance, targeting people thought to be helping the police.  I won't even mention what "necklacing" is, but when they didn't have weapons, they improvised.  

There were some weapons smuggled into South Africa to help the resistance by white South Africans.  Other weapons came from countries like Angola, which did have a connection to Cuba and therefore Russia, and at first a few US politicians used that as an excuse to label the resistance as communists.  But that didn't last long because everyone could see what was happening on the news.  It was a majority black country with white rulers who excluded black people from political representation (which was protested by black leadership to Britain when the government was forming), and they enforced that exclusion with violence.  Whites owned most of the land, the natural resources, and  so on.  The black population was squeezed into little areas called "shantytowns," dense areas of sheds to live in.  (Compare this to the pastoral existence the Xhosa enjoyed before whites arrived.)

Anyway, I could go on for a while, but the point is, South Africa's uprising/revolution doesn't fit the model.  If all revolutions followed the same pattern, we wouldn't be studying history.
 
One more Pam story -- in California, in the 90s, I actually met an older, white South African man at a clubhouse for apartment tenants like myself and the boaters in the complex's marina.  I think he was a boater.  He had gray hair and was physically fit.

He sat with me for a couple of minutes, and I guess he felt comfortable sharing with me that he had trouble finding dates because of what he'd done with the police in South Africa.   (What the... 😶?   Of all the people he could have talked to....)  I sort of gave him a blank stare (my corporate-trained default when I'm shocked).  That was quite an admission ... without me even asking for a thing.  I could have asked him what he'd done, but it was just too much to unwrap, and I'd probably have to hear about him murdering people.

I assumed that he was feeling me out for a possible relationship.  But I wasn't desperate.  I was around 30 years old at the time, and looked much like Grok's image of me on this account's profile -- long, thick, reddish-brown hair down to my butt, turquoise-green eyes, hourglass figure, and usually the prettiest girl in the room.  My biggest problems at the time were my long commute to work, and a rock star's wife and her goons stalking and occasionally trying to kill me because her celeb husband flirted with me occasionally.  I was also well-educated, and a down-to-earth midwesterner who was easy to talk to, coming from outside of L.A.'s cultural hangups on how famous a person was or what they looked like.

I just couldn't think  of anything I wanted to do with the man.  Did I want to open that box and traumatize myself while re-traumatizing him?  Was he looking for a 24/7 psychologist to help him work his way through what he'd done?  Was he still capable of violence?  Would he be violent toward me if I did date him?  Is this how a woman gets into a situation where she turns up missing or d**d?  Honestly, I just couldn't handle it.  I don't even remember what we talked about after that -- just some polite chit-chat for a few moments, then I got up and left.  

South Africa...  it's often something you don't expect.  We can type comments on Elon's posts, knowing that the guy probably has enough money to kills us all, but he's a college-educated nerd who probably knows that bigotry is wrong deep down.  He doesn't seem to be the type of person who'd beat the sh*t out of you just because you're the wrong color, or you pissed him off in some other way.  Maybe his neurodivergence helps, too.  But people who ARE violent over racial issues, or whatever crazy ideas are floating around in their head, do exist, and they're not limited to South Africa.

✈️ PAF’s Mountain Fortress: Why Pakistan Air Force Is Moving Into Swat After Operation Sindoor

“The object of war is not to die for your country, but to make the other bastard die for his.” — George S. Patton

Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra, SYSM, has indicated that on the first night of Operation Sindoor, around 40 Pakistan Air Force aircraft were airborne across the Peshawar–Sargodha axis when the Indian Air Force struck terror infrastructure.

Yet the PAF was unable to prevent the strikes.

Now, Pakistan is reportedly expanding its use of Saidu Sharif Airport in Swat Valley, potentially adding another layer to its airbase network.

✈️ 1. The Peshawar–Sargodha axis

The axis encompasses several important Pakistani air facilities, including Peshawar, Risalpur, Minhas, Chaklala, Mianwali and Sargodha.

The reported presence of around 40 airborne PAF aircraft illustrates the level of activity on the first night of Operation Sindoor.

But numbers in the air are only useful if they can translate into the ability to detect, intercept and prevent an adversary's strike.

🏔️ 2. Why Saidu Sharif matters

Saidu Sharif sits in the Swat Valley, surrounded by mountainous terrain and roughly 150 km from the Line of Control.

Pakistan's apparent interest in the location could provide additional geographical dispersion for its aviation assets and potentially complicate an adversary's targeting picture.

The location also reportedly offers hardened aircraft shelters and facilities capable of supporting aircraft operations.

📡 3. More than just a runway

The significance of an airfield is not determined simply by the number of aircraft it can accommodate.

If configured appropriately, an additional operating location can provide dispersal, refuelling and support options, while potentially allowing airborne early-warning and control aircraft to operate from a less predictable location.

That makes Saidu Sharif potentially relevant to Pakistan's effort to make its air assets harder to neutralise in a future confrontation.

Saidu Sharif may give the PAF another location from which to operate.

It does not make the location invulnerable.

The lesson from Operation Sindoor is simple: moving the runway does not eliminate the threat.

X3705/26

**When the mountain falls, the world answers.**

The 26 August 2026 flash flood that tore through Rasuwa district (Bhotekoshi/Trishuli corridor) near the Tibet border triggered a broad international response.  Multiple countries and organisations have delivered or pledged material, financial and technical support.

**Key verified contributors (as of early September 2026):**

- **India**: Multiple Indian Air Force airlifts delivering tens of tonnes of relief (tents, blankets, medicines, hygiene kits, generators). Specialist tunnel-rescue, medical and forensic teams. Portable Bailey bridges.
- **China**: Several Y-20 military transport flights carrying large volumes of emergency supplies (tents, blankets, morgue freezers, epidemic-prevention materials, daily necessities). Tunnel-rescue experts and identification specialists. Bailey bridges and cash support.
- **United States**: Initial $500,000 emergency funds (later increased), disaster-response adviser, and substantial relief consignments (including 40+ tonnes via partners such as Samaritan’s Purse – water filters, tarpaulins, blankets, solar lights). Food assistance for thousands of households.
- **South Korea**: Prompt response team, $1 million in humanitarian aid, larger disaster-relief team focused on tunnel rescue and forensics. Private commitment (Doosan) of $5 million.
- **Japan**: Emergency relief goods (blankets, plastic sheets, sleeping pads, tents, jerry cans).
- **Australia**: $1 million and approved specialist support.
- **United Kingdom**: £5 million and offered emergency responders.
- **European Union**: €2 million in humanitarian funding, activation of Copernicus satellite monitoring and a Humanitarian Air Bridge.
- **Others**: UAE, Qatar, Singapore, Switzerland, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and several more provided supplies or financial pledges. Multilateral support from the World Bank (large concessional financing), Asian Development Bank ($5 million grant + technical assistance), WHO, UN agencies and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.

Nepal’s Prime Minister publicly thanked India, China, the United States and a long list of other nations and organisations for their solidarity.

Casualty figures remain fluid: latest official tallies stand at approximately **1,252 confirmed dead** and **~4,216 still missing** in Nepal (plus additional losses on the Tibetan side).

Nepal did not face this alone.

Yet the work is far from over. Families still wait. Tunnels still hold secrets. Reconstruction will cost billions. Solidarity is real — but it must now turn into sustained recovery, not just headlines.

The missing still matter. The living still need more than statements.

#NepalFloods #NepalDisaster #Rasuwa #HimalayanTragedy #InternationalAid #ClimateCrisis

X3702/26

**When the mountain comes down, who still flies toward it?**

Ten days after a glacier collapsed and sent a wall of ice, rock and water through the Nepal–Tibet border, the latest official counts stand at **1,252 confirmed dead in Nepal** and approximately **4,216 still listed as missing**. On the Tibetan side, at least **21** have died and over **540** remain unaccounted for. Nearly 12,000 people have been rescued, yet families continue to wait for bodies that may never return. Some have already performed the final rites without a body to bury.

In the wreckage, ordinary people keep choosing risk over safety.

Nepal’s first female helicopter captain, Priya Adhikari, has flown nearly 100 rescue missions in a single week, threading narrow valleys to pull survivors out. A filmmaker turned his drones into search tools, sending them deep into buried hydropower tunnels where conventional teams cannot go. Others who escaped returned to the same danger to help those still trapped.

This is the part of disaster that statistics never fully capture: the decision to go back in. The mother who will never forget the school principal who saved her child. The pilot who keeps taking off when the ground itself has vanished.

The missing still matter. The living still need more than statements.

text:
America Is Entering a Dangerous Era of Institutional Decline

Whatever the ultimate outcome of the war with Iran, the more consequential story may be unfolding inside the United States itself. America is showing signs of institutional deterioration at a pace that should alarm not only Americans, but anyone concerned with global stability.

The United States possesses the world’s most powerful military, an enormous nuclear arsenal, unmatched financial influence, and institutions that for decades were regarded as among the strongest in the democratic world. Yet all of that power is increasingly concentrated around a political system that appears less capable of restraining the impulses of its own president.

Donald Trump’s public behavior illustrates the problem. In roughly an hour, he recently published more than thirty-five posts on his own social media platform, many of them marked by falsehoods, self-obsession, personal attacks, and erratic rhetoric. The issue is not simply one of style or temperament. The deeper question is whether someone who communicates and governs in such a manner should wield such extraordinary executive authority over a country of roughly 350 million people and one of the largest nuclear arsenals on earth.

Healthy political systems are not supposed to depend on the personal discipline of the individual at the top. Their strength lies in institutions capable of constraining leaders when necessary, enforcing rules, protecting public interests, and preventing personal impulses from becoming national policy.

That is precisely where the American system now appears increasingly vulnerable.

A strong constitutional order should be able to restrain a president from pursuing wars driven by personal instinct, from damaging relations with longstanding allies on a whim, or from using public authority in ways that create opportunities for private financial benefit.

Yet concerns over conflicts of interest have become increasingly difficult to dismiss. When a president, his associates, or members of his political circle may financially benefit from market movements influenced by government decisions, the issue goes far beyond political controversy. It becomes a question of institutional integrity.

The same applies to the extraordinary culture of personal loyalty surrounding Trump. Senior officials routinely describe him in language of exaggerated admiration, praising his supposed genius, historic achievements, and singular ability to save the United States and even the wider world. Such rhetoric is more commonly associated with highly personalized political systems than with mature democracies built around institutions rather than individuals.

The erosion is also visible in the relationship between civilian political leadership and professional expertise. Senior military officers have been dismissed, marginalized, or have resigned amid growing tension with political appointees who appear unwilling to tolerate dissenting professional judgment. A system in which expertise is increasingly subordinated to loyalty is a system that gradually loses its capacity for self-correction.

This is what makes the present moment so dangerous.

China and Iran are routinely described in the United States as authoritarian states, while America presents itself as the institutional and democratic alternative. Yet the central advantage of a democracy is not merely the holding of elections. It is the existence of durable institutions capable of limiting power, enforcing accountability, and preventing one person from dominating the state.

If those safeguards cease to function effectively, formal democratic procedures alone offer little protection.

America’s enormous economy will not by itself prevent decline. Nor will military power, technological leadership, or control over global financial networks. History offers many examples of powerful states whose resources remained immense even as their institutions weakened from within.

The real danger, therefore, is not that the United States will suddenly disappear or cease to be a major power. Decline rarely happens that way. More often, it occurs through the gradual normalization of behavior that would once have been considered unacceptable: the politicization of institutions, the weakening of accountability, the elevation of personal loyalty over competence, and the increasing inability of the system to correct its own excesses.

If these trends continue, America may enter a period of accelerated institutional decay whose consequences would extend far beyond its borders.

For that reason, the question facing the rest of the world should no longer be limited to whether the United States will win or lose a particular war, election, or geopolitical confrontation.

A more serious question may soon be unavoidable:

How should the world prepare for a United States that remains extraordinarily powerful, yet becomes increasingly unstable, unpredictable, and institutionally weaker?

Perhaps America can still reverse this trajectory. Removing a president from office through constitutional means, investigating credible allegations of misconduct, prosecuting corruption where evidence justifies it, and restoring institutional independence could all contribute to that process.

But if the current pattern continues unchecked, the problem will no longer be merely American.

The decline of a state with America’s military capabilities, nuclear arsenal, economic weight, and global reach would not be a distant geopolitical event. It would be a source of instability for the entire international system.

For governments, policymakers, and serious observers around the world, it may therefore be time to begin thinking not only about America’s power, but about the consequences of its possible institutional decline.

text:
Mugabe Built Something. That Sentence Should Shame Us.

1). Introductions 
Robert Mugabe died on 6 September 2019. This year, his anniversary falls three days before a date that will matter far more to poor Zimbabweans: 9 September 2026. This is the date when the government’s “zero-tolerance clean-up operation” against street vendors begins in Harare before rolling out nationwide.

Seven years after his death, Zimbabwe’s vendors face a deadline that offers them less than Operation Garikai did.

I hold no brief for Mugabe. He presided over the most violent act of urban policy in our post-independence history. But an honest comparison of May 2005 with September 2026 produces an uncomfortable finding, and it is not the one his admirers want.

2). What 2005 actually did
Operation Murambatsvina began on 18 May 2005. The UN Special Envoy’s report put the number of people who lost homes, livelihoods, or both at more than 700,000, with some 92,000 housing structures destroyed.

Five weeks later the government announced Operation Garikai / Hlalani Kuhle (Stay Well) promising houses and trading stalls for the displaced. Amnesty International documented roughly 3,325 units delivered against those 92,000 demolitions: a replacement rate of 3.6 percent. Implementation ran through committees headed by army personnel, and work published in the Journal of Southern African Studies documented allocation to ruling-party loyalists rather than victims. In 2009 central government handed the sites to broke local councils, where families have now spent fifteen years without sanitation.

 Garikai / Hlalani Kuhle was a smokescreen. 

My argument, however, does not depend on pretending otherwise.

3). The principle that has been abandoned
Here is what Garikai (or Mugabe’s government) nonetheless conceded: that a state which destroys a livelihood incurs an obligation to replace it. The government of 2005 lied about discharging that duty. It did not deny the duty existed. It felt compelled to name a programme and account publicly for the gap.

Compare last week’s notice. Local Government Minister Daniel Garwe gave vendors seven days to vacate undesignated sites, warned that structures would be disbanded and municipal police kept deployed so cleared areas are not reoccupied, and told traders who fail to comply they may lose their merchandise.

The alternative is asserted, but not demonstrated. Nobody has published how many stalls exist, where, or at what rent. Harare registered over 30,000 vendors in earlier rounds and watched most drift back, because the sites had no footfall. A market without customers is not an alternative.

4). The numbers the notice ignores
ZimStat’s Q2 2025 Labour Force Survey puts the informal sector at 58.5 percent of all employed persons and informal employment at 65 percent. Its establishment census found 76.1 percent of the country’s 204,798 operating businesses to be informal. The employment-to-population ratio sits at 37 to 38 percent: fewer than four in ten working-age Zimbabweans hold any job at all, and more than 2.5 million aged 15 to 34 are not in employment, education or training (so called NEETs).

On poverty, use both official measures. Against ZimStat’s estimates that extreme poverty stood at 42 percent when last measured in December 2022. The World Bank’s recently estimated that 49.2 percent of Zimbabweans were extremely poor.

Let’s put these statistics into context: 
What is that line in money? ZimStat’s Food Poverty Line for April 2026 was ZWG909.72 per person per month, which is about US$35 per month or US$1.17 a day. Below that, a person cannot eat.

A vendor’s basin of cucumbers could be worthy $25-40, and that is what stands between her household and the poverty threshold. 1/2

"Purchases over recent months represent a shift in strategy for commercial banks
Dollar deposit rates for some accounts have climbed since June, sources say
Chinese banks keen to seek more profitable assets, sources say
Moves could help slow gains in the yuan.

 Chinese banks have been buying U.S. Treasuries ​over the past few months after lifting dollar deposit rates, according to people familiar with the matter, moves that could help slow gains in the ‌yuan and which come amid a spike in U.S. yields.

For many Chinese banks, U.S. Treasuries represent an attractive investment at a time when yields on Chinese government bonds ​are very low and heavy investment in the domestic bond market has attracted attention from Chinese regulators.

HIKES TO DOLLAR DEPOSIT RATES
Dollar interest rates offered by China's "Big Five" ​state-owned lenders on most deposits have been capped at 2.8% since 2023.
But account holders with balances over $50,000 have been able to negotiate ⁠rates above 3% since June and even close to 4% at some smaller banks or foreign lenders since August, according to a state banker with direct knowledge of the deals.

After paying the deposit rates of 3% to 4%, banks can earn ​income from Treasuries. The 10-year yield has risen more than 30 basis points since the start of June to 4.76%, on a combination of inflation and U.S. debt worries as well as an improved U.S. growth outlook.

MORE DOLLARS IN CHINA
According to banking sources, ‌there is ⁠much more dollar liquidity in China at the moment.

Foreign exchange deposits in China have been rising on the back of booming exports and record trade surpluses. They stood at $1.18 trillion at end-July, up 17.9% from a year earlier and for the first seven months of the year, they grew $121.2 billion, PBOC data showed.

Hikes to dollar deposit rates in China have also meant that keeping money in U.S. dollars, rather than converting it into yuan, has become more attractive. The rate for yuan deposits at major state banks is just 0.95%.

Smaller banks started lifting ​dollar deposit rates in June, forcing larger banks ​to follow suit or lose out on ⁠dollar funding, said another person familiar with the market.
The move coincides with signs China is looking to slow down a rise in its currency as the domestic economy struggles.
Higher deposit rates at banks can soak up dollars and prevent the yuan from rising too fast, the sources ​said. Investing cash abroad also relieves some of the downward pressure on domestic yields.
The yuan is one of the strong currencies ​performing against the dollar, ⁠having gained nearly 9% on the dollar since the beginning of last year. And since the Middle East conflict began at the end of February, China's bond market has been the world's strongest.
.
It ⁠remains to be ​seen whether the banks' recent purchases of U.S. Treasuries will significantly boost China's overall holdings.
The amount of ​Treasuries held by China via U.S. custodians dropped 13% from a year earlier to $633.4 billion in June, the lowest since September 2008 and less than half of a 2013 peak. But the data is regarded as imprecise as ​the ultimate owner of some holdings can be obscured by custody arrangements in centres such as Luxembourg or the Cayman Islands."

text:
🔔🔔Russian Jews of 20th century🧵
_________________________________________
🧵--1

Atthe turn of the 20th century, roughly half the world’s Jews; some 5.2 million souls, lived compressed into the Russian Empire’s Pale of Settlement, a vast cage of legal restrictions, poverty, and recurring violence. Pogroms were not accidents of history. They were policy by another name.

Many fled to America or Palestine long before revolution reshaped the map. Those who stayed would spend the next seven decades inside a Soviet system that promised liberation and delivered a different kind of confinement.

🟢 Crimea

After the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, the Bolsheviks abolished the Pale of Settlement. With funding from the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, tens of thousands of Jewish families relocated to collective farms in Ukraine and Crimea. Traditional Jewish trades: commerce, handicrafts, were deemed unproductive under socialism. The land was the future now.
Crimea already carried deep Jewish memory, older than the Russian Empire, older than the Pale itself.
The Krymchaks had lived on the peninsula since antiquity, descended from Jewish communities that arrived with Greek traders along the Black Sea coast before the Common Era. They spoke Crimean Tatar, dressed like their Tatar neighbors, but kept Rabbinic Judaism strictly; Hebrew prayers, the Talmud, the full calendar of Jewish observance. They simply called themselves “Children of Israel.”

The Crimean Karaites arrived later, with their presence first documented in 1278, though they trace their Jewish roots to ancient Babylon where the Karaite movement was born. They were different from the Krymchaks in one defining way: they accepted the Hebrew Bible but rejected the Talmud entirely, following only the written law. This made them a source of endless debate, were they Jews or something else? The tsars eventually decided the latter, exempting them from anti-Jewish legislation. Most rabbinical authorities considered them a separate branch.

Two communities, both rooted in the same soil for centuries. That depth of Jewish presence is why, after the Revolution, Soviet planners saw Crimea not as an arbitrary choice for Jewish resettlement, but as a return. And it is why, after the war, the Jewish Anti-Fascist Committee would push to make it a Jewish republic. The roots were already there.

Now Jewish settlers carved more than 80 kolkhozes out of the northern steppe, built Yiddish schools, and turned barren land into working farms. Around 200,000 Jews made the move.

“He never talked much about Russia,” recalled Dina Katzman, whose grandfather settled a kolkhoz near Simferopol in 1928. “But when he did, it was always the fields. He said it was the first time in his life nobody could tell him to move on.”

But the dream curdled. Local Crimean Tatars and Slavic communities resisted fiercely. Stalin’s Great Terror swallowed Jewish leaders on charges of bourgeois nationalism. By the late 1930s, the vision of a Jewish republic in Crimea had quietly suffocated.

🟢 Birobidzhan

The Soviet state looked eastward. In 1928 Jews began settling Birobidzhan, a remote, swampy region along the Amur River near the Chinese border. By 1934 it was the Jewish Autonomous Oblast, Yiddish its official language, with its own theaters, newspapers, and schools. The goals: secure a distant border, settle empty land, and offer a socialist alternative to Zionism.

The reality was brutal. The climate was extreme, the land waterlogged, the isolation crushing. Settlers who had imagined a Jewish city found themselves cutting timber in mosquito-filled swamps, hundreds of miles from the nearest town. The Great Purge of 1937–1938 devastated those who stayed. Yosef Liberberg, the region’s first leader, was arrested and shot that year. The Jewish population peaked at around 50,000 before most left. Birobidzhan still exists today as a formal Jewish autonomous region, home to almost no Jews.

🟢 World War II

Then came 1941. The Nazi invasion hunted Jews specifically. More than two million Soviet Jews were murdered, the largest national group killed in the Holocaust. Entire communities that had survived pogroms, revolution, and purges were erased within months.

Soviet Jews also fought back. Up to 500,000 served in the Red Army, the fifth largest group to fall in battle relative to population, a staggering toll for one of the Union’s smallest ethnic groups. More than 150 were awarded Hero of the Soviet Union. Thousands more, estimates range from 20,000 to 30,000; fought as partisans in the forests and marshes of Byelorussia and Ukraine, forming their own units when antisemitism in the broader partisan movement made joining others impossible.

“We fought for the Soviet Union,” said Ilya Ehrenburg, the Jewish-Soviet writer who documented the genocide in real time, “But we also fought for something older than any state, for the right to exist.”

The Soviet government never fully acknowledged the Jewish nature of the Holocaust. The murdered were called “Soviet citizens.” What happened to the Jews specifically was not a story the state wanted told.

After the war, the state actively cultivated a different story: that Jews had avoided military service, hidden behind desks while others bled. It was a slander without basis, the casualty numbers alone gave the lie to it, but it proved durable. The “cowardly Jew” trope, recycled from tsarist propaganda, became a staple of postwar Soviet antisemitism, used to deny Jews credit for their sacrifice and to justify what came next.

🟢 Yalta Conference

In February 1945, with Germany’s defeat weeks away, the three leaders of the Allied powers, Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin, gathered at Yalta on the Crimean coast to divide the postwar world. The fate of nations, borders, and entire peoples was decided across a few days of negotiations. Poland’s future, Germany’s partition, the shape of the United Nations, all were mapped out in those rooms.

Alongside these vast arrangements, Stalin raised what he called the “Jewish problem”, on the very Crimean land where Jewish kolkhozes had once flourished. He described Birobidzhan as the Soviet attempt at a Jewish homeland but admitted it had largely failed. Jews, he said, preferred city life.

Roosevelt declared himself a Zionist and asked if Stalin was one too. “In principle, yes,” Stalin replied. “But I recognize the difficulties.”

Three men dividing the postwar world, pausing to discuss a people who had no seat at the table. After the war, proposals for a Jewish republic in Crimea were rejected. Stalin pushed Jews instead toward Birobidzhan, Kazakhstan, and the Far East.

text:
DID YOU KNOW??

Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, was conceived not just as a deity, but as the literal divine engine and charioteer of Zeus, and her most famous statue was meticulously engineered to create a physical illusion of aerodynamic drag and wind resistance. 

​In Greek mythology, Nike wasn't a standard god; she was a daimon, the anthropomorphic personification of an abstract concept. During the Titanomachy (the cosmic ten-year war for control of the universe), she offered her services to Zeus, acting as the literal engine of his army. She drove his war chariot, granting him the kinetic momentum required to defeat the Titans. This absolute embodiment of speed and aerodynamic force is permanently captured in the Winged Victory of Samothrace, a 2nd-century BC marble masterpiece engineered to sit on the prow of a stone ship. Walk with me 👇🏾👇🏾 

More Surprising Facts About Nike:

A. ​The $35 Swoosh: In 1971, Portland State graphic design student Carolyn Davidson created the famous Nike "swoosh" logo based on the structural shape of the Goddess's wing and the implied sound of aerodynamic speed. She was initially paid just $35 for the design (though the company later gifted her 500 shares of stock).

B. ​The Rolls-Royce Spirit of Ecstasy: The famous hood ornament mounted on the grille of every Rolls-Royce automobile is a direct structural descendant of the Winged Victory of Samothrace, deliberately mimicking her leaning, wind-blown posture to convey silent speed.

C. ​The Olympic Medal Standard: Since the 2004 Athens Games, the International Olympic Committee mandated that the front of every single Summer Olympic medal must feature Nike flying into the Panathenaic Stadium, acting as the permanent visual bridge between ancient Greece and modern athletics.

D. ​The Four Engines of Zeus's Throne: Nike was part of a four-part conceptual engine in Greek mythology. Her siblings were Kratos (Strength), Bia (Force), and Zelus (Zeal or Rivalry). Together, these four physical forces formed the unshakeable foundation of Zeus's power.

SUMMARILY! 
​From the aerodynamic illusions carved into the Winged Victory of Samothrace to her mythological role as the divine engine of Zeus's chariot, Nike represented the physical, unstoppable momentum of triumph that continues to influence modern athletic branding today.
